grade_1.focus: Learning that computers follow simple step-by-step instructions we give them.

lessons.title: What Do Computers Do?
lessons.brief: Computers are machines that follow instructions, just like robots or toys.

lessons.title: Commands: Making Things Happen
lessons.brief: We tell computers what to do using simple commands like 'move', 'stop', 'turn'.

lessons.title: My First Program: A Picture on Screen
lessons.brief: Using a simple tool to make a computer draw or display something we choose.

lessons.title: Mistakes Are Okay: Trying Again
lessons.brief: When our instructions don't work, we can fix them and try a different way.

grade_2.focus: Creating sequences of instructions and watching them make things happen on a screen.

lessons.title: Putting Commands in Order
lessons.brief: Instructions work differently depending on the order we put them in.

lessons.title: Repeat and Patterns
lessons.brief: We can tell a computer to do the same thing over and over to make patterns.

lessons.title: Make a Character Move
lessons.brief: Using sequences of movement commands to make something walk, jump, or dance on screen.

lessons.title: Naming Our Ideas: What is a Program?
lessons.brief: A program is a set of instructions we write for a computer to follow from start to finish.

lessons.title: Bugs: Finding What Went Wrong
lessons.brief: Bugs are mistakes in our programs; we learn to spot and fix them.

grade_3.focus: Understanding how decisions and conditions control what a program does.

lessons.title: If This Happens, Then Do That
lessons.brief: Programs can make choices based on conditions, like 'if the button is pressed, play a sound'.

lessons.title: Yes or No Questions in Code
lessons.brief: Programs ask questions to decide what happens next, using true and false answers.

lessons.title: Loops: Doing Things Again and Again
lessons.brief: Loops let us repeat instructions without writing them many times.

lessons.title: Cause and Effect in Games
lessons.brief: What the player does (cause) makes something happen in the game (effect).

grade_4.focus: Building programs with multiple parts that work together as a system.

lessons.title: Breaking Big Problems into Smaller Parts
lessons.brief: Complex tasks are easier if we divide them into simple, separate instructions.

lessons.title: Variables: Storing and Using Information
lessons.brief: Variables are containers that hold information our program needs to remember and use.

lessons.title: Blocks and Functions: Reusable Instructions
lessons.brief: We can bundle instructions together and use them many times without rewriting them.

lessons.title: How Parts of a Program Connect
lessons.brief: Each part of a program has a job; together they make the whole thing work.

grade_5.focus: Designing programs with clear logic flow and understanding how data moves through systems.

lessons.title: Planning Before We Code: Flowcharts
lessons.brief: Drawing out the path our program will follow helps us write better code.

lessons.title: Data Types: Numbers, Text, and True or False
lessons.brief: Different kinds of information need different types; each has rules for how we use it.

lessons.title: Lists and Collections: Storing Multiple Items
lessons.brief: We can group similar pieces of data together and work with them as one collection.

lessons.title: Why Programs Work or Fail: Testing and Logic
lessons.brief: We test each part of our program to find logical errors before they become big problems.

grade_6.focus: Seeing coding as a way to solve real-world problems and understanding how code connects to other subjects.

lessons.title: Algorithms: Step-by-Step Solutions
lessons.brief: An algorithm is a clear set of instructions for solving any problem, not just computer ones.

lessons.title: Events and Responses: Building Interactive Programs
lessons.brief: Programs can respond to user actions like clicks, typing, or movement in real time.

lessons.title: Efficiency: Making Programs Run Faster and Simpler
lessons.brief: Good coders write programs that use less time and memory by choosing smart algorithms.

lessons.title: Code in the Real World: Apps We Use Every Day
lessons.brief: Understanding what kind of code runs in phones, games, websites, and appliances around us.

grade_7.focus: Understanding coding as a language with history, ethics, and relevance to society.

lessons.title: How Coding Languages Were Born and Evolved
lessons.brief: Different programming languages were created for different reasons and still shape what we can build.

lessons.title: Functions: Writing Your Own Reusable Tools
lessons.brief: Functions let us package logic into named tools that simplify our code and make it readable.

lessons.title: Sorting and Searching: Making Data Useful
lessons.brief: Computers need smart ways to organize and find information quickly in large datasets.

lessons.title: Digital Privacy: What Happens to Data in Programs
lessons.brief: Programs collect and store information about us; understanding this matters for privacy and trust.

grade_8.focus: Evaluating design choices and understanding the trade-offs between different coding approaches.

lessons.title: Debugging Complex Problems: When Things Go Wrong
lessons.brief: Finding and fixing bugs in larger programs requires systematic thinking and patience.

lessons.title: Objects and Classes: Organizing Code Like a Blueprint
lessons.brief: Object-oriented programming lets us model real-world things and organize code into related parts.

lessons.title: Performance vs. Simplicity: Choosing Your Trade-off
lessons.brief: Sometimes fast code is harder to write; we decide what matters most for each project.

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence: Computers That Learn
lessons.brief: AI programs improve by learning from data, but they can inherit human biases and mistakes.

grade_9.focus: Synthesizing multiple coding concepts into larger systems and recognizing patterns across different problems.

lessons.title: Data Structures: Choosing the Right Container
lessons.brief: Arrays, dictionaries, trees, and graphs each solve different problems; choosing wisely matters.

lessons.title: Recursion: Problems That Solve Themselves
lessons.brief: Some problems are elegant when solved by breaking them into smaller versions of the same problem.

lessons.title: APIs: How Programs Talk to Other Programs
lessons.brief: Applications share data and services through APIs, connecting separate systems into larger networks.

lessons.title: Cybersecurity Basics: Protecting Code and Data
lessons.brief: Understanding common vulnerabilities helps us write code that resists attacks and keeps data safe.

grade_10.focus: Interpreting real code from multiple languages and understanding fundamental computer science concepts deeply.

lessons.title: Reading and Analyzing Real-World Code
lessons.brief: Learning to understand code written by others, in different styles and languages, by examining actual projects.

lessons.title: Memory, Pointers, and How Computers Actually Work
lessons.brief: Lower-level understanding of how memory is allocated and used explains why some code is efficient and some is not.

lessons.title: Software Patterns: Proven Solutions to Common Problems
lessons.brief: Design patterns are reusable templates that solve recurring challenges in software design.

lessons.title: Testing Strategies: Writing Programs That Don't Fail
lessons.brief: Unit tests, integration tests, and edge cases are systematic ways to catch errors before deployment.

grade_11.focus: Critiquing code design, comparing frameworks and paradigms, and making independent architectural decisions.

lessons.title: Paradigms Compared: Functional vs. Object-Oriented vs. Procedural
lessons.brief: Different coding styles have different strengths; evaluating them means understanding their trade-offs deeply.

lessons.title: Refactoring: When and How to Rebuild Code
lessons.brief: Good coders improve existing code by identifying weak spots and restructuring without breaking functionality.

lessons.title: Scalability and System Design: From Solo Project to Millions of Users
lessons.brief: Understanding bottlenecks, databases, and distributed systems that let programs grow.

lessons.title: Ethics in Code: Power, Responsibility, and Unintended Consequences
lessons.brief: Code shapes society; examining who benefits, who is harmed, and what responsibilities we have.

grade_12.focus: Conducting independent research into advanced computer science and synthesizing knowledge across theory, practice, and ethics.

lessons.title: Research Project: Investigating a Computer Science Problem
lessons.brief: Students design and execute original research into a computer science topic, reading academic sources and documenting findings.

lessons.title: Complexity Theory: What Problems Can Computers Actually Solve?
lessons.brief: Understanding P vs. NP, computational limits, and why some problems are fundamentally harder than others.

lessons.title: Building a Full-Stack System: From Database to User Interface
lessons.brief: Designing and implementing a complete application demonstrates integration of all coding knowledge.

lessons.title: The Future of Computing: AI, Quantum, and the Unanswered Questions
lessons.brief: Exploring cutting-edge developments and open problems in computer science, and their societal implications.

grade_1.focus: Buildings are real things made of materials that people live, work, and play in.

lessons.title: Homes Around Us
lessons.brief: Learning what a home is and noticing different types of houses in our community.

lessons.title: Parts of a Building
lessons.brief: Identifying and naming the main parts of buildings: walls, doors, windows, roofs, and floors.

lessons.title: Materials Buildings Are Made From
lessons.brief: Touching and observing real materials like wood, brick, stone, and glass used in construction.

lessons.title: Buildings Do Different Jobs
lessons.brief: Exploring how different buildings serve different purposes: schools, shops, hospitals, and playgrounds.

grade_2.focus: Buildings have shapes and designs that are made by architects and builders working together.

lessons.title: How Architects Design Buildings
lessons.brief: Learning that architects draw plans before buildings are built and deciding where things go.

lessons.title: Shapes and Spaces Inside Buildings
lessons.brief: Noticing how rooms are different shapes and sizes and how they connect to each other.

lessons.title: Building Tools and Jobs
lessons.brief: Meeting the different workers involved in building and the tools they use on site.

lessons.title: Decorating the Outside
lessons.brief: Observing how buildings look different on the outside through colors, patterns, and details.

grade_3.focus: Buildings are designed to meet people's needs by organizing spaces and materials in smart ways.

lessons.title: Sorting Buildings by Type and Purpose
lessons.brief: Categorizing buildings by their function and comparing how form follows what people need to do inside.

lessons.title: How Weather Shapes Building Design
lessons.brief: Understanding why buildings in hot, cold, wet, and windy places are designed differently.

lessons.title: Basic Structures: Walls, Columns, and Beams
lessons.brief: Learning how buildings stand up using different structural systems and what each one does.

lessons.title: Planning Spaces for People
lessons.brief: Exploring how architects arrange rooms and pathways to make buildings easy and safe to move through.

grade_4.focus: Buildings are systems where structure, materials, function, and human use all work together as a whole.

lessons.title: How Load and Structure Work Together
lessons.brief: Understanding how weight moves through buildings and why certain shapes and materials support buildings better.

lessons.title: The Architect's Toolkit: Drawings and Plans
lessons.brief: Reading and creating simple floor plans, elevations, and sections to communicate design ideas.

lessons.title: Sustainable Materials and Building Choices
lessons.brief: Investigating how material choice affects the environment and how buildings can be built responsibly.

lessons.title: Designing for Different Users and Needs
lessons.brief: Analyzing how architects consider age, ability, and culture when planning spaces for communities.

grade_5.focus: Architectural design solves real-world problems by balancing technical constraints, materials, site conditions, and human needs.

lessons.title: From Site Analysis to Design Decision
lessons.brief: Learning how architects study a location's climate, terrain, and existing surroundings before designing a building.

lessons.title: Structural Systems and Their Limits
lessons.brief: Examining different structural approaches—frames, shells, trusses—and how each has advantages and constraints.

lessons.title: Circulation and Movement Through Space
lessons.brief: Tracing how people move through buildings and how architects intentionally design pathways, stairs, and connections.

lessons.title: Building Codes and Regulations Shape Design
lessons.brief: Discovering how safety rules, accessibility standards, and local laws influence what architects can and must do.

grade_6.focus: Architecture is an interconnected discipline where design decisions reflect cultural values, environmental responsibility, economic constraints, and innovation in technology.

lessons.title: How Culture and Context Shape Architecture
lessons.brief: Analyzing how architecture across different regions reflects climate, available materials, traditions, and social values.

lessons.title: Analyzing Architectural Styles and Their Evolution
lessons.brief: Comparing design approaches across history and identifying how technology, materials, and philosophy changed buildings over time.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Energy, Water, and Waste in Buildings
lessons.brief: Understanding how buildings interact with natural systems and designing solutions for efficiency and minimal environmental impact.

lessons.title: Adaptive Reuse and Resilient Design
lessons.brief: Exploring how architects modify old buildings for new purposes and design buildings to withstand change and stress.

grade_7.focus: Buildings are designed solutions to human needs, and different cultures and climates produce different architectural styles.

lessons.title: Why Buildings Look Different Across the World
lessons.brief: Explores how climate, available materials, and cultural values shape the appearance and function of buildings in different regions.

lessons.title: Reading a Building Like a Story
lessons.brief: Teaches students to observe and describe architectural elements—columns, arches, roofs, windows—and understand what each part does.

lessons.title: From Sketch to Structure: How Architects Plan
lessons.brief: Introduces the design process, including sketching, blueprints, and models, and how architects communicate ideas to builders.

lessons.title: Public Spaces That Bring People Together
lessons.brief: Examines how plazas, markets, parks, and gathering spaces are deliberately designed to encourage community interaction.

grade_8.focus: Architecture reflects and shapes the values, power, and beliefs of the societies that create it.

lessons.title: Monuments, Memory, and Who Gets to Decide
lessons.brief: Investigates how buildings and monuments are used to celebrate certain histories and whose stories are included or excluded.

lessons.title: Sacred Spaces: How Religion and Architecture Connect
lessons.brief: Analyzes how temples, mosques, churches, and other religious buildings express spiritual beliefs through design and symbolism.

lessons.title: Palaces, Fortresses, and the Architecture of Power
lessons.brief: Examines how rulers and governments use grand, imposing, or strategically placed buildings to demonstrate authority and control.

lessons.title: Whose City? Access, Exclusion, and Urban Design
lessons.brief: Explores how architectural decisions about walls, gates, gated communities, and public versus private spaces reflect and create social inequality.

grade_9.focus: Architecture is both an art and a system; it must balance aesthetic vision, practical constraints, and human impact.

lessons.title: The Tension Between Vision and Reality in Design
lessons.brief: Examines how architects balance creative ambition with budget, engineering limits, local regulations, and client needs.

lessons.title: Modernism's Promise: Can Design Fix Society?
lessons.brief: Analyzes the modernist belief that good design could improve daily life, and evaluates both successes and failures of this approach.

lessons.title: Building for the Body: How Scale and Proportion Affect How We Feel
lessons.brief: Studies the relationship between human physiology and architectural proportions, and how buildings can comfort or alienate occupants.

lessons.title: Sustainability and the Cost of Building
lessons.brief: Investigates the environmental and social impact of construction materials, energy use, and the tension between durability and efficiency.

grade_10.focus: Architectural movements emerge from specific historical moments; understanding context is essential to evaluating architecture's role in society.

lessons.title: Gothic and Renaissance: How Changing Ideas Produced New Forms
lessons.brief: Traces how shifts in religion, humanism, and technology drove architectural innovation and what buildings reveal about their era's worldview.

lessons.title: Industrial Revolution and the Birth of Modern Architecture
lessons.brief: Examines how new materials (iron, steel, concrete) and manufacturing enabled radically different building types and urban expansion.

lessons.title: The Bauhaus: Where Art, Craft, and Function Collide
lessons.brief: Analyzes this influential design school's attempt to unify aesthetics and utility, and its lasting impact on modernist architecture.

lessons.title: Colonialism and the Architecture of Empire
lessons.brief: Studies how colonizing powers used architecture to assert dominance, displace local building traditions, and embed cultural hierarchies.

grade_11.focus: Architectural theory frameworks compete to explain what architecture *is* and *should be*—aesthetics, function, meaning, and ethics are never neutral.

lessons.title: Functionalism vs. Symbolism: What Should a Building Express?
lessons.brief: Compares theories that prioritize utility and logic against those that emphasize meaning, emotion, and cultural narrative in architectural form.

lessons.title: Postmodernism's Critique: Irony, Pastiche, and the Death of Grand Narratives
lessons.brief: Evaluates postmodern architects' rejection of modernism's utopian ideals and their use of historical reference, humor, and complexity.

lessons.title: Architecture and Identity: Design as Political Act
lessons.brief: Analyzes how architects have used design to assert cultural identity, resist erasure, and challenge dominant power structures.

lessons.title: The Global Spread of Architectural Style: Homogenization or Dialogue?
lessons.brief: Examines whether globalization has created a uniform international architecture or enabled new forms of cultural exchange and hybridization.

grade_12.focus: Architecture operates at the intersection of art, science, politics, and ethics; independent research and argumentation reveal its complexity and stakes.

lessons.title: Reading Primary Sources: How Architects Defend Their Work
lessons.brief: Develops skills in analyzing architects' own writings, manifestos, and interviews to understand intention versus interpretation and reception.

lessons.title: Case Study Analysis: Tracing Design Decisions Through Constraints
lessons.brief: Conducts detailed research into a single building's or urban project's genesis, stakeholders, compromises, and unintended consequences.

lessons.title: Architecture in Crisis: Climate, Justice, and the Future of Building
lessons.brief: Synthesizes current debates about sustainable design, housing inequity, and climate adaptation to construct evidence-based arguments about responsible architecture.

lessons.title: Proposing Architecture: From Critique to Vision
lessons.brief: Develops independent research questions and designs a speculative architectural response grounded in theory, historical precedent, and ethical reasoning.

grade_1.focus: Art is all around us — we can see, touch, and describe colours, shapes, and objects that artists make.

lessons.title: Colours and Feelings
lessons.brief: Learn how different colours make us feel happy, calm, sad, or excited.

lessons.title: Shapes in Pictures
lessons.brief: Find circles, squares, triangles, and other shapes in real artwork and in the world.

lessons.title: What Artists Use to Make Art
lessons.brief: Explore paint, pencils, clay, and other materials artists use to create.

grade_2.focus: Artists use colours, shapes, and materials to show things they see and feel, and we can tell stories by looking at art.

lessons.title: How Artists Show Movement
lessons.brief: See how artists draw or paint people and animals running, jumping, and playing.

lessons.title: Details That Tell Stories
lessons.brief: Look closely at paintings to find small things that help us understand what is happening.

lessons.title: Making Art from Nature
lessons.brief: Discover how artists use flowers, leaves, rocks, and animals as subjects in their work.

lessons.title: Light and Shadow in Art
lessons.brief: Notice how artists show where light comes from and where shadows fall in pictures.

grade_3.focus: Different artists and cultures make art in different ways, and we can compare and sort art by style, purpose, and time period.

lessons.title: Portraits: How Artists Show People
lessons.brief: Compare portrait paintings from different artists and periods to see how faces are painted differently.

lessons.title: Why Did Ancient People Make Art?
lessons.brief: Explore cave paintings and early sculptures to understand what people used art for long ago.

lessons.title: Warm and Cool Colours in Different Paintings
lessons.brief: Sort and compare artworks to see how artists choose warm or cool colours for different moods and purposes.

lessons.title: Symmetry and Pattern in Art
lessons.brief: Find repeated shapes and balanced designs in decorative art, textiles, and architecture.

grade_4.focus: Art movements and styles are connected to how artists solve problems and how the world around them changes, using composition, technique, and intention.

lessons.title: How the Renaissance Changed Painting: Perspective and Depth
lessons.brief: Learn how artists discovered perspective to make flat pictures look three-dimensional and realistic.

lessons.title: The Role of Composition: Arranging the Picture
lessons.brief: Analyze how artists position subjects, use lines, and guide the viewer's eye through a painting.

lessons.title: From Nature to Symbol: What Objects Mean in Art
lessons.brief: Explore how fruit, flowers, animals, and everyday objects carry hidden meanings in paintings.

lessons.title: Techniques Across Cultures: Ink Painting, Fresco, and Oil
lessons.brief: Compare how different cultures and time periods developed distinct painting methods and materials.

grade_5.focus: Art movements emerge from historical moments and cultural shifts; artists develop techniques and styles to respond to society, religion, politics, and personal vision.

lessons.title: Power and Propaganda: How Art Was Used by Rulers and States
lessons.brief: Examine how monarchs, religious institutions, and governments commissioned art to show authority and spread ideas.

lessons.title: The Industrial Revolution and Its Effect on Art: From Realism to Impressionism
lessons.brief: Trace how factories, cities, and new technology changed what artists painted and how they painted it.

lessons.title: Technique and Expression: Brushwork, Colour, and the Artist's Hand
lessons.brief: Analyze how artists developed personal techniques and visible brushstrokes to convey emotion and authenticity.

lessons.title: Global Trade and Artistic Exchange: Japanese Influence on Western Painting
lessons.brief: Investigate how artists in Europe were inspired by Japanese prints and how cultural contact shapes style.

grade_6.focus: Art reflects and shapes culture; major movements emerge from philosophical, technological, and social forces, and artists challenge convention to express meaning in their time.

lessons.title: Modernism and the Rejection of Realism: Why Picasso, Kandinsky, and Others Broke the Rules
lessons.brief: Explore how artists in the early 20th century abandoned literal representation to express abstraction, psychology, and inner experience.

lessons.title: Art and Politics: Propaganda, Resistance, and Activism in Visual Culture
lessons.brief: Analyze how artists responded to war, fascism, colonialism, and injustice through symbolic and provocative imagery.

lessons.title: The Artist's Process: Studio Practice, Experimentation, and the Evolution of Style
lessons.brief: Examine how individual artists developed their style over time through deliberate choices and formal experimentation.

lessons.title: Intersections: How Technology, Gender, and Globalisation Shaped Contemporary Art
lessons.brief: Consider how photography, film, new media, and questions of identity changed who could be an artist and what art could express.

grade_7.focus: Art history as a mirror of human culture: how artists document, celebrate, and challenge the worlds they live in.

lessons.title: Why Societies Build Monuments
lessons.brief: Explores how ancient civilisations used monumental art and architecture to express power, belief, and identity.

lessons.title: Art as Storytelling Across Cultures
lessons.brief: Examines how different cultures—Egyptian, Greek, African, Indigenous—use visual art to preserve and transmit stories.

lessons.title: The Medieval Church and Artistic Control
lessons.brief: Investigates how religious institutions shaped what artists could create and why certain subjects dominated medieval art.

lessons.title: Trade Routes and Artistic Exchange
lessons.brief: Traces how the Silk Road and maritime trade spread artistic techniques and styles between distant civilisations.

grade_8.focus: The Renaissance and Enlightenment as pivotal moments when artists began asking new questions about art's purpose, human potential, and scientific truth.

lessons.title: Perspective, Anatomy, and Humanism: What Changed in Renaissance Art
lessons.brief: Analyzes how artists like da Vinci and Michelangelo combined scientific observation with artistic innovation to represent humans and space differently.

lessons.title: Who Paid for Art and Why It Mattered
lessons.brief: Examines the role of patrons—church, nobility, merchants—in determining what art was made and what messages it conveyed.

lessons.title: Art and Propaganda: The Medici, the Papacy, and Political Power
lessons.brief: Evaluates how ruling families and institutions commissioned art to reinforce authority, legitimacy, and ideology.

lessons.title: Craft, Genius, and the Birth of the 'Artist'
lessons.brief: Investigates how the Renaissance elevated the status of artists from craftspeople to creative visionaries, and the consequences of that shift.

grade_9.focus: Modernism as a break from tradition: how industrialisation, new materials, photography, and global conflict forced artists to reinvent what art could be and say.

lessons.title: Photography and the Crisis of Representation
lessons.brief: Examines how the invention of photography challenged painters' role as documenters of reality and prompted new artistic directions.

lessons.title: Revolution in Form: Cubism, Abstraction, and the Rejection of Realism
lessons.brief: Synthesizes how Picasso, Kandinsky, and others dismantled representational conventions to explore emotion, form, and perception.

lessons.title: Art and the Machinery of War: Dada, Surrealism, and Political Art
lessons.brief: Explores how World Wars, fascism, and social upheaval prompted artists to use absurdism, symbolism, and protest to critique society.

lessons.title: Materials and Meaning: How Modernists Expanded What Could Be Art
lessons.brief: Analyzes how artists moved beyond paint and canvas to use found objects, new media, and unconventional surfaces to challenge definitions of art.

grade_10.focus: Post-modernism and contemporary art: artists questioning the very frameworks modernism created, engaging identity, mass culture, and the power structures embedded in art institutions.

lessons.title: Deconstructing the Masterpiece: Feminist and Postcolonial Critiques
lessons.brief: Reads primary texts and artworks by feminist and postcolonial artists to examine whose stories art history tells and who is excluded.

lessons.title: Pop Art and the Blurred Line Between Fine Art and Consumer Culture
lessons.brief: Interprets how Warhol, Lichtenstein, and others appropriated advertising and mass production to interrogate authenticity and value.

lessons.title: Institutional Critique: When Artists Question the Gallery Itself
lessons.brief: Analyzes works that expose the gallery, museum, and market as ideological spaces, not neutral containers for art.

lessons.title: Identity, Representation, and the Body in Contemporary Art
lessons.brief: Examines how artists use their own bodies and identities—race, gender, sexuality—as material and critique in response to historical erasure.

grade_11.focus: Comparative art-historical frameworks: how different theoretical lenses—formalist, Marxist, psychoanalytic, poststructuralist—produce competing interpretations of the same work.

lessons.title: Formalism vs. Content: Does How Art Looks Matter More Than What It Says?
lessons.brief: Critically examines Greenberg's formalist theory against socially engaged interpretations, using specific artworks to test each framework's strengths and limitations.

lessons.title: Marxist Art History: Reading Class and Labor Into the Canvas
lessons.brief: Applies Marxist analysis to Renaissance workshops, industrial-era art, and capitalist commodity culture to expose economic structures art both reflects and resists.

lessons.title: Psychoanalysis, the Unconscious, and Surrealism: Freud Meets Artistic Practice
lessons.brief: Critiques Freudian and Lacanian readings of Surrealist and contemporary work, evaluating the validity and limitations of depth psychology in art interpretation.

lessons.title: Constructing the Canon: Who Decides What Art History Is?
lessons.brief: Investigates how taste, institutional power, and historical bias have canonized certain artists and movements while marginalizing others, and argues for alternative histories.

grade_12.focus: Synthesis and independent research: students develop original arguments about art history using primary sources, theoretical frameworks, and cross-disciplinary evidence, preparing for scholarly inquiry.

lessons.title: Primary Source Analysis: Reading Manifestos, Letters, and Artist Statements as Historical Evidence
lessons.brief: Develops skills in close reading of manifestos and artist writings; students learn to contextualize claims and recognize authorial bias.

lessons.title: Global Art Histories: Decentering the European Canon and Rethinking Periodization
lessons.brief: Examines non-Western and Indigenous art traditions on their own terms, critiques Eurocentric periodization, and synthesizes multiple simultaneous art histories.

lessons.title: Art as Archive and Resistance: How Artists Document, Preserve, and Challenge Power
lessons.brief: Conducts research into contemporary and historical artists who use art as a tool of memory, witness, and political resistance; students develop evidence-based arguments about efficacy.

lessons.title: Independent Inquiry: Designing and Defending an Original Art-Historical Argument
lessons.brief: Students formulate a research question, gather primary and secondary sources, apply theoretical frameworks, and write a sustained argument that contributes new insight.

grade_1.focus: The Sun, Moon, and stars are real things in the sky that change and move.

lessons.title: Day and Night
lessons.brief: Learning that the Sun makes daytime and its absence makes nighttime.

lessons.title: The Moon Changes Shape
lessons.brief: Observing and naming the different shapes the Moon appears to have each night.

lessons.title: Stars Twinkle and Stay Still
lessons.brief: Discovering that stars are tiny lights far away that appear the same every night.

grade_2.focus: The Earth is a place where day and night happen, and the Sun and Moon move across the sky in patterns.

lessons.title: The Sun Moves Across the Sky
lessons.brief: Tracking the Sun's path from morning to evening and noticing it appears in different places.

lessons.title: Why the Moon Looks Different Each Night
lessons.brief: Learning that the Moon's shape changes because we see different amounts of sunlight on it.

lessons.title: Seasons Change What We See
lessons.brief: Observing that the Sun is higher or lower in the sky at different times of year, making it warmer or colder.

lessons.title: Constellations: Pictures Made of Stars
lessons.brief: Identifying star patterns in the night sky and learning that people have named them for thousands of years.

grade_3.focus: The Earth orbits the Sun and rotates on its axis, which explains day, night, seasons, and the Moon's phases.

lessons.title: How Earth's Spin Creates Day and Night
lessons.brief: Understanding that Earth rotates like a spinning top, causing different parts to face the Sun at different times.

lessons.title: Earth's Year-Long Path Around the Sun
lessons.brief: Learning that Earth orbits the Sun and this journey creates the four seasons.

lessons.title: The Moon Orbits Earth
lessons.brief: Discovering that the Moon travels around Earth and its position changes what we see from night to night.

lessons.title: Planets Are Worlds Like Earth
lessons.brief: Identifying other planets in our Solar System and comparing them to Earth in size and distance from the Sun.

grade_4.focus: Our Solar System is an organized collection of objects orbiting the Sun, each with distinct properties and behaviors.

lessons.title: The Solar System's Architecture
lessons.brief: Mapping the positions and relative distances of planets, moons, and other objects orbiting the Sun.

lessons.title: Inner and Outer Planets: Two Worlds
lessons.brief: Comparing rocky terrestrial planets near the Sun with gas giants farther away, and explaining their different characteristics.

lessons.title: Gravity Keeps Orbits Going
lessons.brief: Learning how the Sun's gravitational pull holds planets and moons in their orbits.

lessons.title: Comets, Asteroids, and Meteorites
lessons.brief: Identifying different small bodies in space and explaining what happens when they enter Earth's atmosphere.

grade_5.focus: Stars have lifecycles, the Sun is a star, and the universe contains billions of stars organized into galaxies.

lessons.title: The Sun: Our Local Star
lessons.brief: Examining the Sun's structure, energy production through nuclear fusion, and its role in powering life on Earth.

lessons.title: How Stars Are Born and Die
lessons.brief: Tracing a star's lifecycle from formation in nebulae through main sequence to red giant, white dwarf, or supernova.

lessons.title: Measuring Distances to the Stars
lessons.brief: Learning why stars appear small and how light-years let us measure the vast distances between Earth and distant stars.

lessons.title: Galaxies and the Milky Way
lessons.brief: Understanding that our Solar System sits within the Milky Way galaxy, one of billions of galaxies in the universe.

grade_6.focus: The universe is vast, ancient, and governed by physics; we understand it through observation, evidence, and interconnected scientific concepts.

lessons.title: Reading the Sun's Spectrum
lessons.brief: Using spectroscopy to determine a star's temperature, composition, and motion, and applying this to understand stellar properties.

lessons.title: The Life and Death of Massive Stars
lessons.brief: Analyzing how stellar mass determines evolution path, comparing outcomes such as neutron stars and black holes.

lessons.title: The Expanding Universe and the Big Bang
lessons.brief: Exploring evidence that the universe is expanding and what that tells us about its ancient origin and ultimate fate.

lessons.title: Exoplanets and the Search for Life
lessons.brief: Examining how we detect planets around other stars and evaluating the conditions needed for life beyond Earth.

grade_7.focus: The solar system as a dynamic place where celestial mechanics and human exploration intersect.

lessons.title: Why Planets Stay in Orbit
lessons.brief: Gravity as the force that holds the solar system together and keeps planets in stable paths around the Sun.

lessons.title: The Lived Experience of Astronauts
lessons.brief: What happens to the human body in space and how astronauts prepare for and survive in microgravity.

lessons.title: Mapping the Moons and Their Discoveries
lessons.brief: The moons of our solar system as worlds in their own right, from Europa's hidden ocean to Saturn's Titan.

lessons.title: Space Probes as Messengers
lessons.brief: How unmanned spacecraft extend human exploration beyond Earth and what they have revealed about other planets.

grade_8.focus: Competing theories about planetary origins and the evidence astronomers use to decide between them.

lessons.title: How the Solar System Was Born
lessons.brief: The nebular hypothesis and the evidence from meteorites, isotopes, and planetary structure that supports or challenges it.

lessons.title: The Great Debate: Where Did the Moon Come From?
lessons.brief: Evaluating three competing theories of lunar origin (fission, capture, and giant impact) against observational evidence.

lessons.title: Why Mars Lost Its Atmosphere and Earth Kept Its
lessons.brief: How planetary mass, magnetic fields, and solar wind explain why some planets retain atmospheres while others don't.

lessons.title: Reading the Record in Craters and Canyons
lessons.brief: How geological features on planetary surfaces reveal the history of impacts, volcanism, and planetary change.

grade_9.focus: The life cycles of stars and how stellar physics determines the fate of planetary systems.

lessons.title: The Main Sequence: Why Stars Spend Most of Their Lives Burning Hydrogen
lessons.brief: Stellar equilibrium, the balance between gravity and fusion pressure, and why this phase lasts billions of years.

lessons.title: Death of a Star and Birth of Its Remnants
lessons.brief: White dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes as the end products of stellar evolution, determined by mass.

lessons.title: Habitability Across Stellar Lifetimes
lessons.brief: How a star's age, luminosity, and stability affect the conditions for life on orbiting planets over cosmic time.

lessons.title: Reading Light from Distant Stars
lessons.brief: Spectroscopy and the electromagnetic spectrum as tools to measure stellar composition, temperature, and motion.

grade_10.focus: The detection and characterization of exoplanets, and what they tell us about planetary formation and habitability.

lessons.title: Transit Method and Radial Velocity: How We Find Worlds We Cannot See
lessons.brief: The physics and mathematics behind two major exoplanet detection techniques and their respective strengths and biases.

lessons.title: The Architecture of Exoplanetary Systems
lessons.brief: Why exoplanet systems have unexpected configurations, and how orbital resonances, migration, and instability shape them.

lessons.title: Biosignatures and False Positives
lessons.brief: Which atmospheric gases hint at life, which abiotic processes mimic them, and how future telescopes will distinguish them.

lessons.title: The Goldilocks Problem: Redefining the Habitable Zone
lessons.brief: How stellar type, planetary composition, atmospheric effects, and orbital stability reframe what 'habitable' actually means.

grade_11.focus: Cosmology and the origin, evolution, and ultimate fate of the universe itself, grounded in observation and competing models.

lessons.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background as a Fossil Record
lessons.brief: How the CMB provides evidence for the Big Bang, and how analysis of temperature fluctuations constrains models of the early universe.

lessons.title: Dark Matter and Dark Energy: Crisis or Framework?
lessons.brief: Critical evaluation of evidence for unseen components of the universe, including alternative explanations like modified gravity.

lessons.title: The Expansion of Space and the Cosmic Distance Ladder
lessons.brief: How astronomers measure cosmic distances, determine the Hubble constant, and reconcile conflicting measurements.

lessons.title: Nucleosynthesis: How Stars Built the Periodic Table
lessons.brief: Tracing the origin of elements from the Big Bang through stellar fusion, supernovae, and neutron star mergers.

grade_12.focus: Current unsolved questions in cosmology and astrobiology, with emphasis on methodology, evidence gaps, and competing research frameworks.

lessons.title: The Hubble Tension and Crisis in Cosmological Measurements
lessons.brief: Examining conflicting measurements of expansion rate, their sources of uncertainty, and proposals to resolve the discrepancy.

lessons.title: Gravitational Waves as a New Window on the Universe
lessons.brief: The physics of gravitational wave detection, what LIGO has revealed about mergers and neutron stars, and future observatories.

lessons.title: Panspermia, Abiogenesis, and the Statistical Case for Extraterrestrial Life
lessons.brief: Evaluating evidence for different pathways to life, the Drake equation, and why consensus remains elusive despite exoplanet discoveries.

lessons.title: Research Methods in Observational Cosmology
lessons.brief: Conducting original analysis of real astronomical datasets, understanding systematic errors, peer review, and the sociology of scientific debate.

grade_1.focus: Living things are all around us, and we can observe what they look like, where they live, and what they need to grow.

lessons.title: What Is Alive?
lessons.brief: Students learn to identify living things (animals and plants) and non-living things in their everyday world.

lessons.title: Where Do Animals Live?
lessons.brief: Students explore different habitats (homes) where animals live, such as forests, water, and gardens.

lessons.title: What Do Plants and Animals Need?
lessons.brief: Students discover that all living things need food, water, air, and light (or warmth) to survive.

lessons.title: My Body, Your Body
lessons.brief: Students identify and name the basic parts of their own body and how they move and sense the world.

grade_2.focus: Living things have different body parts that help them survive, and each plant and animal is suited to its home.

lessons.title: Plant Parts and What They Do
lessons.brief: Students learn that roots take in water, stems hold plants up, leaves make food, and flowers make seeds.

lessons.title: Animal Bodies: Coverings and Movement
lessons.brief: Students observe that animals have different skin, fur, or scales, and different ways of moving (walking, swimming, flying).

lessons.title: Babies Grow Into Adults
lessons.brief: Students trace how baby animals and plants grow bigger and change into their adult forms.

lessons.title: Staying Safe and Healthy
lessons.brief: Students learn how their bodies protect them (skin, bones) and how to keep their bodies clean and strong.

grade_3.focus: Living things are classified into groups based on their features, and each organism has a life cycle.

lessons.title: Sorting Animals: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
lessons.brief: Students classify animals based on whether they have a backbone and group them into categories like mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish.

lessons.title: Plant Families and How They Reproduce
lessons.brief: Students compare flowering plants and non-flowering plants, and learn how seeds and spores help plants spread.

lessons.title: Life Cycles: From Egg to Adult
lessons.brief: Students follow the complete life cycle of insects (egg, larva, pupa, adult), frogs (egg, tadpole, froglet, frog), and mammals.

lessons.title: Predators, Prey, and Food Chains
lessons.brief: Students discover that animals eat plants or other animals, and trace simple food chains in a habitat.

grade_4.focus: Organisms interact within ecosystems through energy flow and nutrient cycles, and their bodies are made of specialized systems.

lessons.title: Ecosystems: Producers, Consumers, and Decomposers
lessons.brief: Students understand how plants produce energy from the sun, animals consume that energy, and decomposers return nutrients to soil.

lessons.title: Body Systems Working Together
lessons.brief: Students learn how the skeletal, muscular, digestive, respiratory, and circulatory systems work together to keep an organism alive.

lessons.title: How Animals Adapt to Their Habitats
lessons.brief: Students examine how physical features (camouflage, sharp teeth, long necks) and behaviors help animals survive in their specific environments.

lessons.title: The Water and Carbon Cycles
lessons.brief: Students trace how water and carbon move through living things and the environment in repeating cycles.

grade_5.focus: Cells are the basic unit of life, organisms inherit traits, and populations change over time through natural selection.

lessons.title: Cells: Structure and Function
lessons.brief: Students examine plant and animal cells under a microscope, identify key organelles, and understand that all living things are made of cells.

lessons.title: Inheritance and Variation in Populations
lessons.brief: Students investigate how offspring inherit traits from parents, how variation exists within populations, and how this variation matters for survival.

lessons.title: Evolution and Natural Selection
lessons.brief: Students analyze fossil evidence and real examples to understand how organisms with helpful traits are more likely to survive and pass traits to offspring.

lessons.title: Energy Flow Through Living Systems
lessons.brief: Students trace how energy from the sun is captured by plants, transferred through food chains, and used by organisms for growth and movement.

grade_6.focus: Life is organized at multiple scales from molecules to biomes, and human systems interact with broader biological processes.

lessons.title: Molecular Basis of Life: DNA and Proteins
lessons.brief: Students learn how DNA stores genetic instructions, how genes are expressed, and how proteins are built and carry out life functions.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration: Energy Transformation
lessons.brief: Students analyze how plants convert light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis, and how all organisms release that energy through respiration.

lessons.title: Population Ecology and Ecosystem Balance
lessons.brief: Students model how population size is controlled by birth rates, death rates, and resources, and predict how changes in one species affect entire ecosystems.

lessons.title: Human Impact on Biodiversity and Cycles
lessons.brief: Students evaluate how human activities alter nutrient cycles, habitats, and species diversity, and consider conservation strategies.

grade_7.focus: How living things are organized into systems that work together to keep organisms alive.

lessons.title: Cells: The Basic Unit of Life
lessons.brief: Students learn that all living things are made of cells, explore cell structures and their functions, and understand why cells are considered the smallest unit of life.

lessons.title: How Organs and Systems Keep Us Working
lessons.brief: Students trace how different body systems (digestive, circulatory, respiratory) work together to transform food into energy and distribute it throughout the body.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration: Two Sides of Energy
lessons.brief: Students discover how plants capture light energy to make food while all organisms break down food for energy, and why these processes are connected.

lessons.title: Reproduction: Passing Life Forward
lessons.brief: Students compare sexual and asexual reproduction, explore why organisms reproduce, and examine how traits pass from parents to offspring.

grade_8.focus: Why organisms have the traits they do, and how living things adapt to their environments over time.

lessons.title: What Traits Really Are: Genes, Environment, and Chance
lessons.brief: Students examine why siblings differ even with the same parents, explore which traits are inherited versus shaped by environment, and debate the limits of each.

lessons.title: Darwin's Argument: How Evolution Explains Diversity
lessons.brief: Students work through Darwin's logic using evidence from fossils, breeding, and anatomy, and evaluate how well his explanation accounts for what we observe in nature.

lessons.title: Adaptation in Action: Real Examples of Organisms Solving Problems
lessons.brief: Students analyze specific adaptations (camouflage, migration, body shape) as solutions to survival challenges, and consider alternative explanations for why organisms have them.

lessons.title: Evidence for Evolution: What Fossils, DNA, and Living Things Tell Us
lessons.brief: Students examine multiple independent lines of evidence for evolution and learn why scientists consider this evidence convincing, while acknowledging gaps in the record.

grade_9.focus: How populations change across generations, and the mechanisms that drive or constrain evolution.

lessons.title: Heredity at the Molecular Level: How DNA Codes for Traits
lessons.brief: Students learn how genes are segments of DNA, how DNA replicates and gets passed on, and how mutations create variation that natural selection acts upon.

lessons.title: Population Genetics: Why Some Traits Become Common and Others Disappear
lessons.brief: Students model allele frequencies in populations, explore how selection, migration, and drift change populations over time, and predict which traits will persist.

lessons.title: Speciation: When Populations Become Different Species
lessons.brief: Students investigate reproductive isolation, examine case studies of speciation, and synthesize how genetic change and geographic separation produce new species.

lessons.title: The Tree of Life: Evidence That All Organisms Share Common Ancestors
lessons.brief: Students construct and interpret phylogenetic trees using morphological and genetic data, and connect evolutionary relationships to the diversity of life on Earth.

grade_10.focus: How evolution has shaped the structure and function of organisms at every scale, and how to evaluate competing scientific claims about evolutionary processes.

lessons.title: Comparing Body Plans: Homology, Analogy, and What They Reveal
lessons.brief: Students analyze homologous and analogous structures across species, interpret what these similarities suggest about common ancestry, and evaluate alternative interpretations of structural similarities.

lessons.title: Molecular Evolution: Using DNA and Protein Sequences to Trace Descent
lessons.brief: Students learn how DNA differences accumulate over time, calculate evolutionary distance between species using genetic data, and compare molecular and morphological approaches to reconstructing evolutionary history.

lessons.title: Natural Selection, Genetic Drift, and Gene Flow: When Does Each Matter Most?
lessons.brief: Students model conditions under which selection dominates versus drift, examine empirical examples where different mechanisms explain population change, and evaluate which mechanism best explains specific evolutionary scenarios.

lessons.title: Constraints and Trade-offs: Why Evolution Doesn't Produce Perfect Organisms
lessons.brief: Students explore why organisms have limitations (developmental pathways, historical baggage, energetic constraints), examine case studies of suboptimal design, and develop arguments about what this reveals about the evolutionary process.

grade_11.focus: Evaluating competing hypotheses about how evolution works at multiple scales, and synthesizing evidence from diverse sources to build arguments about evolutionary mechanisms.

lessons.title: Testing Adaptive Hypotheses: When Is a Trait an Adaptation, and When Do We Just Not Know?
lessons.brief: Students learn the criteria for identifying adaptations, critique published studies claiming traits are adaptive, and construct rigorous arguments distinguishing adaptation from exaptation, byproduct, or neutral variation.

lessons.title: Macroevolution vs. Microevolution: Can Small Changes Add Up?
lessons.brief: Students evaluate the debate over whether mechanisms visible in populations (selection, drift) sufficiently explain large-scale diversity, synthesize fossil and genetic evidence, and build independent arguments about the sufficiency of modern evolutionary theory.

lessons.title: Convergent and Divergent Evolution: Independent Solutions to Similar Problems
lessons.brief: Students analyze cases where unrelated organisms evolved similar traits, critique hypotheses explaining convergence, and use comparative methods to infer selection pressures and developmental constraints across lineages.

lessons.title: Human Evolution: Reading the Evidence and Evaluating Competing Narratives
lessons.brief: Students examine primary fossil, genetic, and anatomical data on human origins, evaluate competing interpretations of the hominin fossil record, and assess how cultural and scientific bias may shape evolutionary narratives.

grade_12.focus: Conducting original analysis of evolutionary questions using multiple data sources, critiquing the philosophy and practice of evolutionary biology, and applying evolutionary thinking to contemporary problems.

lessons.title: Phylogenetic Inference: Building and Interpreting Trees from Real Data
lessons.brief: Students work with published sequence alignments and morphological datasets, construct phylogenies using parsimony and likelihood methods, evaluate support for different topologies, and understand assumptions underlying tree-building algorithms.

lessons.title: The Modern Synthesis and Its Challengers: What Mechanisms Really Drive Evolution?
lessons.brief: Students read primary literature on neo-Darwinism, epigenetics, evolutionary developmental biology, and other frameworks; evaluate evidence for and against each; and synthesize a reasoned position on which mechanisms matter most for explaining biological diversity.

lessons.title: Evolution in Real Time: Analyzing Rapid Evolutionary Change in Populations
lessons.brief: Students examine case studies of evolution happening in weeks to decades (bacteria, insects, finches), analyze the data critically, and argue about what rapid evolution reveals about the power and limits of evolutionary mechanisms.

lessons.title: Applying Evolution: From Antibiotic Resistance to Conservation to Medicine
lessons.brief: Students research how evolutionary principles predict and explain real-world phenomena, design solutions to problems grounded in evolutionary reasoning, and evaluate the ethical and practical implications of applying evolutionary science.

grade_1.focus: Everything is made of stuff that we can see, touch, smell, and taste.

lessons.title: What Things Are Made Of
lessons.brief: Explore that all objects around us—rocks, water, food, air—are made of something.

lessons.title: Hot, Cold, Hard, Soft
lessons.brief: Describe how materials feel and change when they are heated or cooled.

lessons.title: Mixing and Stirring
lessons.brief: Observe what happens when we mix different things together like sand and water or salt and sugar.

grade_2.focus: Materials have different properties and can change when we do things to them.

lessons.title: Solids, Liquids, and Air
lessons.brief: Name and describe the three forms of matter using everyday examples like ice, water, and steam.

lessons.title: When Things Dissolve
lessons.brief: Watch salt and sugar dissolve in water and see how some things disappear but the mixture changes.

lessons.title: Melting and Freezing
lessons.brief: Observe how ice melts into water and how water freezes back into ice when temperature changes.

lessons.title: Burning and Rusting
lessons.brief: Notice that some materials change permanently when they burn or rust and cannot easily go back.

grade_3.focus: Materials can be sorted by their properties, and chemical reactions cause lasting changes that are different from physical changes.

lessons.title: Grouping Materials by Properties
lessons.brief: Sort and compare materials like wood, plastic, metal, and glass by how they look, feel, and behave.

lessons.title: Reversible Changes: Freezing, Melting, and Dissolving
lessons.brief: Identify changes that can be undone—ice melting back to water, salt dissolving and reappearing when water evaporates.

lessons.title: Irreversible Changes: Cooking and Burning
lessons.brief: Observe that cooking an egg or burning paper creates something completely new that cannot change back.

lessons.title: Acids and Bases in Everyday Life
lessons.brief: Test whether common substances like lemon juice, soap, and vinegar are acids or bases using simple indicators.

grade_4.focus: Elements combine in specific ways to form compounds, and chemical reactions rearrange atoms to create new substances.

lessons.title: Elements: The Building Blocks of Matter
lessons.brief: Learn that all matter is made from about 100 elements, and recognize common ones like oxygen, hydrogen, carbon, and nitrogen.

lessons.title: Atoms and Simple Molecules
lessons.brief: Understand that atoms are tiny particles that join together to form molecules, and model molecules like water and oxygen.

lessons.title: How Compounds Form
lessons.brief: Discover that when elements combine chemically, they form compounds with completely different properties than the elements alone.

lessons.title: Signs of a Chemical Reaction
lessons.brief: Recognize that bubbling, color change, heat release, and new smells indicate that a chemical reaction has occurred.

grade_5.focus: Chemical reactions follow patterns and rules; energy is released or absorbed during reactions, and the same atoms are rearranged but never lost.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Chemical Equations
lessons.brief: Learn to represent reactions symbolically so that we can see which atoms start on one side and end up on the other.

lessons.title: Energy in Reactions: Exothermic and Endothermic
lessons.brief: Investigate reactions that release heat (burning, rusting) and reactions that absorb heat (dissolving salt in water).

lessons.title: The Law of Conservation of Mass
lessons.brief: Measure reactants and products to prove that mass is never created or destroyed, only rearranged during a reaction.

lessons.title: Rates of Reaction
lessons.brief: Experiment with temperature, particle size, and concentration to understand what makes some reactions happen faster than others.

grade_6.focus: Chemical reactions involve energy transfer and are governed by predictable rules; atoms rearrange to form new bonds, and we can model and predict reaction behavior.

lessons.title: Bonding: How Atoms Stick Together
lessons.brief: Understand ionic and covalent bonds at a basic level, and explain why different compounds have different properties based on how their atoms bond.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Combustion
lessons.brief: Analyze burning and rusting as oxidation reactions, and explore the role of oxygen and energy in these common exothermic processes.

lessons.title: Acid-Base Reactions and pH
lessons.brief: Test the pH of solutions using indicators, predict what happens when acids and bases meet, and explain neutralization reactions.

lessons.title: Predicting and Balancing Reactions
lessons.brief: Use patterns and the periodic table to predict products of simple reactions and balance equations to show atom conservation.

grade_7.focus: Matter has structure: atoms and elements are the building blocks of everything we see and use.

lessons.title: What Are Atoms and Why Do They Matter?
lessons.brief: Students discover that all matter is made of atoms, explore the basic structure of atoms, and see why atoms are the smallest unit that matters.

lessons.title: The Periodic Table: A Map of Elements
lessons.brief: Students learn how elements are organised by properties, use the periodic table to find information, and understand why some elements behave similarly.

lessons.title: Bonding: How Atoms Stick Together
lessons.brief: Students explore how atoms combine to form compounds, distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds, and see how bonding explains the properties of everyday materials.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions: Matter Transforms
lessons.brief: Students observe that chemical reactions rearrange atoms to create new substances, write simple equations, and learn that matter is conserved in reactions.

grade_8.focus: Chemical reactions follow patterns and rules; understanding these patterns explains why reactions happen and predicts what will form.

lessons.title: Types of Chemical Reactions and How to Predict Them
lessons.brief: Students categorise reactions as combustion, acid–base, and displacement; learn predictive patterns; and apply these to explain real-world reactions.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases, and the pH Scale
lessons.brief: Students investigate what makes something acidic or basic, measure pH in common substances, and understand how acid–base reactions are used in industry and safety.

lessons.title: Energy in Chemical Reactions
lessons.brief: Students explore exothermic and endothermic reactions, measure energy release or absorption, and connect this to why some reactions are useful for heat or fuel.

lessons.title: Rates of Reaction: Speed and Control
lessons.brief: Students investigate what changes how fast a reaction happens (temperature, concentration, surface area), design experiments to test variables, and apply this to real processes.

grade_9.focus: Atoms and molecules behave according to quantifiable laws; we can measure, calculate, and predict chemical change using molar relationships and stoichiometry.

lessons.title: The Mole: Counting Atoms and Molecules
lessons.brief: Students learn why the mole is essential for chemistry, convert between grams and moles, and see how to scale from individual particles to measurable quantities.

lessons.title: Stoichiometry: Predicting Amounts in Reactions
lessons.brief: Students use balanced equations and molar ratios to predict how much product forms or reactant is needed, solve limiting reactant problems, and check their answers with percent yield.

lessons.title: Solutions and Concentration
lessons.brief: Students learn how solutes dissolve in solvents, calculate molarity and other concentration measures, and explore how concentration affects reaction rates and properties.

lessons.title: Electron Arrangement and Periodic Trends
lessons.brief: Students examine electron configurations, understand why periodic trends (ionisation energy, electronegativity, atomic radius) exist, and predict element behaviour from position on the table.

grade_10.focus: Bonding and molecular structure determine physical and chemical properties; we can explain macroscopic behaviour using particle-level models.

lessons.title: Ionic Bonding and Ionic Compound Properties
lessons.brief: Students examine electron transfer, draw ionic structures, and connect ionic bonding to properties like high melting points, solubility in polar solvents, and electrical conductivity when molten.

lessons.title: Covalent Bonding and Molecular Shape
lessons.brief: Students explore electron sharing, use VSEPR theory to predict 3D shapes, and show how molecular geometry influences properties like polarity and intermolecular forces.

lessons.title: Intermolecular Forces and Physical Properties
lessons.brief: Students distinguish between intramolecular bonds and intermolecular forces (dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding), explain why substances have different boiling points and solubilities, and connect to real applications.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Redox Reactions
lessons.brief: Students assign oxidation numbers, identify oxidation and reduction, balance redox equations, and explore electron transfer in combustion, corrosion, and electrochemistry.

grade_11.focus: Chemical systems move toward equilibrium; we can model and predict the direction and extent of reaction using thermodynamics and equilibrium principles.

lessons.title: Thermodynamics: Enthalpy, Entropy, and Spontaneity
lessons.brief: Students calculate enthalpy changes, explore entropy and disorder, apply Gibbs free energy to predict whether reactions are spontaneous, and critique why some non-spontaneous reactions are driven forward.

lessons.title: Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible Reactions and Le Chatelier's Principle
lessons.brief: Students write equilibrium expressions, calculate equilibrium constants, apply Le Chatelier's principle to predict shifts, and argue how industrial processes (Haber process, contact process) exploit equilibrium.

lessons.title: Acid–Base Equilibria and Buffer Systems
lessons.brief: Students examine Ka and Kb, calculate pH of weak acids and bases, design buffer solutions, and analyse how buffers resist pH change—linking to blood pH and laboratory chemistry.

lessons.title: Kinetics and Reaction Mechanisms
lessons.brief: Students distinguish between reaction rate and mechanism, use collision theory and activation energy to explain rate laws, propose mechanisms consistent with experimental data, and evaluate competing models.

grade_12.focus: Chemical behaviour emerges from quantum mechanics and molecular interactions; students synthesise thermodynamics, kinetics, and equilibrium to solve complex, real-world problems.

lessons.title: Quantum Mechanics and Bonding Models
lessons.brief: Students examine orbital theory, molecular orbital diagrams, and resonance structures; critique limitations of classical models; and connect quantum predictions to experimental bond properties and reactivity.

lessons.title: Electrochemistry: Cells, Spontaneity, and Electricity
lessons.brief: Students calculate cell potentials using standard reduction potentials, link electrochemistry to thermodynamics, design galvanic and electrolytic cells, and analyse real applications (batteries, corrosion prevention).

lessons.title: Organic Chemistry: Structure, Reaction, and Synthesis
lessons.brief: Students name and draw organic molecules, predict reaction outcomes using mechanistic reasoning, design multi-step syntheses, and evaluate green chemistry alternatives to traditional methods.

lessons.title: Integration Project: Designing a Chemical System
lessons.brief: Students synthesise thermodynamics, kinetics, equilibrium, and electrochemistry to design, optimise, and critically analyse a real or hypothetical industrial or laboratory chemical process, presenting evidence-based arguments for their choices.

grade_1.focus: Learning the names and basic moves of each chess piece.

lessons.title: The Chess Board and How to Set It Up
lessons.brief: Students learn the 64 squares, the light and dark pattern, and where each piece belongs at the start of a game.

lessons.title: How the Pawns Move
lessons.brief: Students discover that pawns move forward one square (or two on their first move) and capture diagonally.

lessons.title: How the Rooks, Bishops, and Queens Move
lessons.brief: Students learn that rooks move in straight lines, bishops move diagonally, and the queen moves both ways.

lessons.title: How the King and Knight Move
lessons.brief: Students find out that the king moves one square in any direction and the knight jumps in an L-shape.

grade_2.focus: Playing simple games and learning why some pieces are more valuable than others.

lessons.title: The Value of Each Piece
lessons.brief: Students learn that pieces are worth different amounts—pawns are worth 1, rooks worth 5, and the queen worth 9.

lessons.title: What It Means to Capture and Trade
lessons.brief: Students practice taking opponent pieces and learn when a trade is fair (same value) or unfair (losing more than you gain).

lessons.title: Playing Your First Game from Start to Finish
lessons.brief: Students play a complete game using all the moves they have learned, with a teacher guiding them.

lessons.title: Protecting Your Pieces
lessons.brief: Students learn that pieces can defend each other and that leaving a piece undefended is a mistake.

grade_3.focus: Understanding how pieces work together and recognizing basic patterns of threat and safety.

lessons.title: Checkmate: When the King Has No Escape
lessons.brief: Students learn the rule that ends a game—when a king is under attack and has no safe move.

lessons.title: Check, Pins, and Skewers
lessons.brief: Students discover that pieces can attack the king (check), trap a piece against the king (pin), or attack two pieces in a line (skewer).

lessons.title: Controlling the Centre of the Board
lessons.brief: Students see that the four middle squares are important territory and that pieces placed there are stronger.

lessons.title: Pawn Promotion and the Back Rank
lessons.brief: Students learn that pawns become queens when they reach the far end and why the back row matters for king safety.

grade_4.focus: Developing pieces at the start of a game and learning how opening principles build a strong position.

lessons.title: The Opening: Moving Towards the Centre First
lessons.brief: Students learn that the first moves should control the middle squares before moving pieces that are already developed.

lessons.title: Developing All Your Pieces Before Attacking
lessons.brief: Students understand that moving the same piece twice in the opening is slow, and that getting knights, bishops, and rooks into play first is a system.

lessons.title: Castling: The King's Escape Route
lessons.brief: Students learn the castling move—a special move that moves the king to safety and brings the rook into the game at once.

lessons.title: Recognizing Forks, Pins, and Double Attacks
lessons.brief: Students categorise tactical patterns and see how to create positions where one move attacks two pieces or forces an opponent's response.

grade_5.focus: Learning why the opening, middle game, and endgame each have different goals and how to transition between them.

lessons.title: Pawn Structure: How Pawns Shape Your Position
lessons.brief: Students trace how pawn moves create long-term weaknesses or strengths and learn that fixing broken pawn structures is hard.

lessons.title: The Middle Game: Creating Threats and Finding Combinations
lessons.brief: Students learn sequences of moves (combinations) where each move supports the next to create an advantage or checkmate.

lessons.title: Piece Activity and Tempo in Play
lessons.brief: Students analyse how quickly pieces reach good squares, how many threats one player can create, and why moving faster (tempo) can win material or position.

lessons.title: Endgame Basics: When Only Kings, Pawns, and Few Pieces Remain
lessons.brief: Students learn that in the endgame, pawn promotion becomes the main goal, and king activity (not safety) becomes essential.

grade_6.focus: Analysing deep positions, understanding strategic plans, and recognising how position type determines what each side should do.

lessons.title: Trading Pieces as a Strategic Choice
lessons.brief: Students learn that simplifying into a winning endgame is often the best strategy, and that some players should trade while others should not.

lessons.title: Weak Squares and Long-Term Advantage
lessons.brief: Students identify squares that cannot be defended by pawns and see how controlling those squares (especially near the enemy king) builds lasting pressure.

lessons.title: Evaluating Positions: Material, Safety, Activity, and Structure
lessons.brief: Students learn to weigh multiple factors (how much material each side has, king safety, piece mobility, and pawn formations) to judge if a position is winning, drawn, or losing.

lessons.title: Famous Games and What They Teach About Strategy
lessons.brief: Students study classical games to see how masters plan moves ten steps ahead, sacrifice material for positional advantage, and convert small advantages into wins.

grade_7.focus: Chess as a tool for strategic thinking: learning how to plan moves ahead, recognize patterns, and understand why top players make the decisions they do.

lessons.title: The Calculation Chain: How Deep Do You Need to Think?
lessons.brief: Students learn to calculate variations systematically and discover that depth of analysis matters more than looking at every possible move.

lessons.title: Pattern Recognition in the Middlegame
lessons.brief: Identifying recurring tactical themes (pins, forks, skewers, discovered attacks) that appear across different positions and how to spot them quickly.

lessons.title: Tournament Play and Sportsmanship
lessons.brief: The culture of competitive chess: how tournaments work, the ethics of play, and how professional players handle pressure and defeat.

grade_8.focus: Evaluating competing strategic ideas: learning that multiple valid plans can exist in one position, and how to weigh which approach is strongest in context.

lessons.title: Space Control vs. Material: When Is Each Worth More?
lessons.brief: Analyzing positions where one side has more pieces but less space, and learning to evaluate which advantage is decisive in different circumstances.

lessons.title: The Pawn Structure Debate
lessons.brief: How pawn formations create long-term advantages or weaknesses, and how different players interpret the same pawn structure in opposing ways.

lessons.title: Preparation vs. Creativity in Opening Choice
lessons.brief: Examining why some players memorize lines while others choose less-studied moves; evaluating the trade-offs between safety and originality.

lessons.title: Endgame Principles: Rules or Guidelines?
lessons.brief: Testing classical endgame rules (e.g., 'the king is strong in the endgame') against positions where the opposite is true.

grade_9.focus: Building a personal decision-making framework: synthesizing tactical awareness, strategic understanding, and position evaluation into a coherent approach to choosing moves.

lessons.title: Position Assessment: Creating Your Own Evaluation
lessons.brief: Moving beyond memorized assessments to develop an independent method for judging whether a position favors White, Black, or is equal—and why.

lessons.title: The Move Selection Process: From Candidate Moves to Decision
lessons.brief: Following the thought process of strong players: generating candidate moves, calculating their consequences, and selecting the move that aligns with your goals.

lessons.title: Psychological Elements in Chess: Risk, Confidence, and Playing Style
lessons.brief: How personality, confidence, and personal risk tolerance influence move choice, and how top players adapt their style to their opponent and the match situation.

lessons.title: Chess History as a Laboratory for Ideas
lessons.brief: Using historical games and players (Kasparov, Fischer, Karpov, Anand) to understand how chess philosophy has evolved and what these paradigm shifts reveal about the game.

grade_10.focus: Critical interpretation of chess authority: reading historical sources, contemporary analysis, and computer evaluations with a skeptical eye, and understanding their limitations.

lessons.title: Reading Classical Game Annotations: Bias and Insight
lessons.brief: Examining how annotators from different eras and styles explained their games; identifying where personal narrative, ego, or limited understanding shaped their interpretations.

lessons.title: Computer Chess vs. Human Understanding
lessons.brief: Exploring what chess engines reveal (and what they obscure): when engine lines are practical, when they miss human nuance, and how to use silicon without becoming enslaved to it.

lessons.title: Opening Theory: Assumptions Built Into Systems
lessons.brief: Analyzing how opening principles (control the center, develop quickly, castle early) became dogma, and examining the positions and players that challenged or confirmed them.

lessons.title: Comparative Analysis: The Same Position, Multiple Verdicts
lessons.brief: Taking a single complex position and examining how different sources (classical books, modern engines, contemporary grandmasters) evaluate it differently—and why.

grade_11.focus: Advanced critique and synthesis: analyzing competing chess philosophies, evaluating evidence for strategic claims, and constructing independent arguments about how chess should be understood and played.

lessons.title: Romantic vs. Scientific Chess: Competing Frameworks for Understanding the Game
lessons.brief: Contrasting the intuitive, aggressive style of 19th-century chess with the systematic, positional approach of the Hypermoderns; evaluating which framework explains superior performance.

lessons.title: The Evolution of Pawn Play: From Silence to Centrality
lessons.brief: Tracing how pawn structure went from overlooked to paramount in chess thinking; analyzing the games and theories that drove this shift and its limitations.

lessons.title: Preparation and Innovation: How Do Players Genuinely Create New Chess?
lessons.brief: Examining how top players move beyond preparation to produce original ideas in openings and middlegames; analyzing the tension between knowledge and discovery.

lessons.title: Constructing a Chess Worldview: Building Your Own Analytical Framework
lessons.brief: Synthesizing lessons from history, theory, and analysis to articulate a personal, evidence-based philosophy of what chess is and how it should be approached.

grade_12.focus: Original research and synthesis at pre-university level: conducting independent investigation into chess history, theory, or practice, and producing a rigorous argument that draws on evidence across multiple domains.

lessons.title: Research Seminar: Investigating an Unsettled Question in Chess
lessons.brief: Students select a disputed claim or puzzle in chess history (e.g., the true assessment of a famous position, the origins of a strategic principle, or a player's legacy) and conduct original research.

lessons.title: Chess and Cognition: What the Game Reveals About Human Decision-Making
lessons.brief: Synthesizing chess analysis with research from psychology and neuroscience to examine how and why chess players make choices, and what this tells us about expertise.

lessons.title: The Ethics and Philosophy of Chess: Beyond the 64 Squares
lessons.brief: Examining chess as a model of fair competition, strategic thinking, and intellectual culture; considering questions of equity, access, and what chess teaches about how to live.

grade_1.focus: Learning who helps us in our community and what they do every day.

lessons.title: People Who Help Us
lessons.brief: Meeting community helpers like teachers, firefighters, and doctors and learning what they do.

lessons.title: My Family and Home
lessons.brief: Understanding family members, household rules, and how families work together.

lessons.title: Our School Community
lessons.brief: Exploring the school building, school rules, and the different jobs people do at school.

lessons.title: Being a Good Neighbour
lessons.brief: Learning how to be kind, share, and help others in daily life.
