lessons.brief: Computing derivatives using rules, interpreting them as slopes and rates, and applying to maximization problems and particle motion.

lessons.title: Integration and Accumulation: Area Under Curves
lessons.brief: Developing the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums, proving the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and computing antiderivatives.

lessons.title: Differential Equations and Mathematical Modeling
lessons.brief: Setting up and solving differential equations to model phenomena in physics, biology, and economics; interpreting solutions qualitatively and quantitatively.

lessons.title: Proof Techniques and Mathematical Argumentation
lessons.brief: Constructing rigorous proofs by contradiction, contrapositive, and induction; critiquing mathematical arguments for validity and logical coherence.

grade_1.focus: Media is all around us—pictures, sounds, and words that tell us things.

lessons.title: What Is Media All Around Me?
lessons.brief: Students identify different types of media in their everyday life: books, TV, photos, music, and signs.

lessons.title: Pictures Tell Stories
lessons.brief: Students learn that images communicate ideas and feelings without words.

lessons.title: Sounds and Voices Carry Messages
lessons.brief: Students explore how music, speech, and sound effects create mood and meaning.

grade_2.focus: Different media use different tools to share messages with us.

lessons.title: How Books, Screens, and Speakers Work Differently
lessons.brief: Students compare how books, tablets, TVs, and radios each deliver information in their own way.

lessons.title: Colors, Words, and Sounds Make Us Feel Things
lessons.brief: Students examine how creators choose colors, language, and audio to create specific emotions.

lessons.title: Real Photos and Drawings Tell Different Kinds of Truth
lessons.brief: Students distinguish between photographs (showing real moments) and drawings or animations (showing ideas).

lessons.title: Who Makes Media and Why?
lessons.brief: Students learn that real people create media to share, teach, entertain, or sell things.

grade_3.focus: Media is created on purpose—every choice a creator makes affects what we see and feel.

lessons.title: Spotting the Creator's Choices
lessons.brief: Students identify decisions creators make (what to show, what to hide, which words to use, which music to add) and why those choices matter.

lessons.title: Advertisements Are Designed to Persuade
lessons.brief: Students analyze how ads use familiar people, bright colors, catchy songs, and special words to convince us to buy things.

lessons.title: Fact, Opinion, and Made-Up Stories in Media
lessons.brief: Students learn to sort information into what is true, what someone believes, and what is pretend.

lessons.title: How Different Media Audiences See Things Differently
lessons.brief: Students explore how a news story, cartoon, or movie about the same event can tell very different versions.

grade_4.focus: Media systems connect creators, messages, and audiences—and each part affects the others.

lessons.title: The Media Chain: From Creator to You
lessons.brief: Students trace how media moves from the person who makes it, through companies and platforms, to reach audiences.

lessons.title: How Money Shapes What Media Gets Made
lessons.brief: Students examine how advertising, subscriptions, and sponsorships influence what stories are told and how they are told.

lessons.title: Bias in the Frame: What Creators Choose to Show and Hide
lessons.brief: Students analyze how camera angles, editing, music placement, and word choice reveal a creator's perspective and can shape belief.

lessons.title: Spreading, Sharing, and Changing: How Media Moves Online
lessons.brief: Students learn how digital platforms allow media to spread quickly, get remixed, and transform as people share and comment.

grade_5.focus: Media shapes how we understand the world—and understanding media helps us think more clearly.

lessons.title: Narrative Techniques: How Creators Build Stories That Stick
lessons.brief: Students examine pacing, character development, conflict, and resolution to understand how structure influences emotional impact and memory.

lessons.title: Statistics, Data, and Manipulation: When Numbers Lie
lessons.brief: Students learn how graphs, percentages, and data visualizations can be designed to mislead and how to evaluate claims critically.

lessons.title: Identity and Representation: Whose Stories Get Told?
lessons.brief: Students analyze which groups appear in media, how they are portrayed, and what messages that sends about who matters and belongs.

lessons.title: Fact-Checking and Tracing Information Back to Its Source
lessons.brief: Students develop strategies to verify claims, find original sources, and recognize when information has been taken out of context.

grade_6.focus: Media is a system of power—understanding it means recognizing whose interests are served and what alternatives exist.

lessons.title: Ownership Structures and Concentration: Who Controls What We See
lessons.brief: Students investigate how a small number of corporations own many media outlets and how that concentration affects diversity of voices and viewpoints.

lessons.title: Algorithmic Curation: How Platforms Decide What You See
lessons.brief: Students explore how recommendation algorithms and content feeds operate, what signals they optimize for, and how they can create filter bubbles.

lessons.title: Manipulation Tactics: Emotional Triggers, Deepfakes, and Disinformation
lessons.brief: Students analyze deliberate techniques used to exploit attention, spread false information, and manufacture outrage across media ecosystems.

lessons.title: Alternative Media and Counter-Narratives: Creating and Finding Other Stories
lessons.brief: Students examine independent media, community platforms, and marginalized creators as sources of perspectives excluded from mainstream outlets.

grade_7.focus: How media messages are constructed and designed to influence audiences.

lessons.title: Spotting the Sell: Advertising Techniques in Everyday Media
lessons.brief: Students identify common persuasion tactics (celebrity endorsement, emotional appeals, bandwagon effect) in ads across platforms.

lessons.title: The People Behind the Screen: Who Creates Media and Why
lessons.brief: Students explore media ownership, business models, and how profit motives shape what stories get told.

lessons.title: Fact or Fiction: Separating News from Propaganda
lessons.brief: Students learn criteria for evaluating news sources and recognize propaganda techniques like loaded language and selective reporting.

lessons.title: Images That Lie: How Photos and Video Can Deceive
lessons.brief: Students examine how cropping, editing, filters, and context manipulation change the truth a visual tells.

grade_8.focus: Evaluating competing claims and understanding bias in how stories are framed.

lessons.title: Bias in the Newsroom: Why the Same Event Gets Told Different Ways
lessons.brief: Students compare coverage of one event across outlets with different political leanings and identify what gets emphasized or omitted.

lessons.title: Following the Money: How Funding Shapes Media Content
lessons.brief: Students trace sponsorships, advertising revenue, and corporate ownership to understand financial incentives behind media choices.

lessons.title: Deepfakes and Digital Manipulation: When You Can't Trust Your Eyes
lessons.brief: Students learn how synthetic media is created and why it's dangerous, and practice spotting signs of manipulation.

lessons.title: Echo Chambers and Algorithms: Why Your Feed Shows You What It Does
lessons.brief: Students investigate how social media algorithms personalize content and how this affects what information they see.

grade_9.focus: Analyzing how media narratives shape identity, power, and social beliefs.

lessons.title: Representation and Stereotypes: Who Gets Shown, and How
lessons.brief: Students examine patterns in how gender, race, class, and other identities are portrayed across genres and platforms, and what impact this has.

lessons.title: Power and Voice: Whose Stories Get Told and Whose Are Missing
lessons.brief: Students investigate structural barriers to media creation and distribution, and analyze whose perspectives dominate mainstream narratives.

lessons.title: Misinformation Ecosystems: How False Claims Spread and Why People Believe Them
lessons.brief: Students map how misinformation moves through networks, examine cognitive biases that make people susceptible, and evaluate fact-checking strategies.

lessons.title: Media Literacy Across Cultures: How Different Countries Frame the Same Issues
lessons.brief: Students compare how media systems in different countries operate and how cultural context shapes what is considered newsworthy or true.

grade_10.focus: Interpreting original media texts and sources to construct informed arguments about media's role in society.

lessons.title: Deconstructing Documentary: How Filmmakers Use Technique to Build Arguments
lessons.brief: Students analyze how cinematography, music, narration, and editing in documentaries construct claims, and evaluate whether evidence supports conclusions.

lessons.title: The Rhetoric of Social Media: Persuasion Tactics in Posts, Stories, and Influencer Culture
lessons.brief: Students study how influencers and activists use platform-specific conventions to build authority and mobilize audiences, and critique their claims.

lessons.title: Primary Sources in a Digital Age: Evaluating Credibility When Anyone Can Publish
lessons.brief: Students develop frameworks for assessing authority, bias, and reliability in original documents, datasets, and user-generated content.

lessons.title: Media Regulation and Free Speech: Balancing Rights, Harm, and Access
lessons.brief: Students examine different regulatory models globally, analyze the tension between censorship and protection, and form informed positions on media policy.

grade_11.focus: Critiquing competing frameworks for understanding media power and synthesizing arguments about media's role in democracy.

lessons.title: Marxist, Liberal, and Libertarian Theories of Media: Which Framework Explains Reality Best?
lessons.brief: Students study foundational theories about media ownership and control, compare their explanatory power, and evaluate their limitations.

lessons.title: Agenda-Setting vs. Gatekeeping vs. Spiral of Silence: Competing Models of Media Influence
lessons.brief: Students analyze case studies through multiple theoretical lenses to determine which best explains how media shapes public opinion.

lessons.title: Media Literacy as Resistance: Critical Consumption, Production, and Activism
lessons.brief: Students examine media literacy as a political practice, evaluate counter-narratives and independent media, and develop personal media philosophies.

lessons.title: The Attention Economy: How Platform Design Weaponizes Human Psychology
lessons.brief: Students investigate behavioral design, algorithmic manipulation, and data harvesting, and argue whether regulation or individual choice is the answer.

grade_12.focus: Conducting original research on media systems and producing evidence-based arguments about media's future and ethical responsibilities.

lessons.title: Research Design in Media Studies: Collecting and Analyzing Data About Media Consumption and Effects
lessons.brief: Students design and execute small-scale research projects (content analysis, surveys, interviews) on media phenomena and interpret findings critically.

lessons.title: Platform Ecosystems: How Tech Giants Shape Information, Power, and Democracy
lessons.brief: Students research the business models, algorithms, and policies of major platforms, synthesize evidence of their societal impact, and argue positions on regulation.

lessons.title: Media Ethics and Responsibility: Professional Standards, Corporate Accountability, and Public Trust
lessons.brief: Students examine ethical frameworks used by journalists and creators, analyze case studies of ethical failures, and develop their own media ethics position.

lessons.title: The Future of Truth: Synthesizing Media Literacy for an Era of AI, Synthetic Media, and Information Chaos
lessons.brief: Students synthesize learning across the curriculum to make forward-looking arguments about how media literacy must evolve and what new literacies are emerging.

grade_1.focus: Sound is everywhere—learning to listen, make sounds, and play simple instruments.

lessons.title: Sounds All Around Us
lessons.brief: Students identify and name sounds in their environment: birds, rain, doors, voices.

lessons.title: High and Low: Pitch Games
lessons.brief: Students explore how sounds can be high (like a whistle) or low (like a drum) and practice making both.

lessons.title: Loud and Soft: Volume Exploration
lessons.brief: Students learn that sounds can be loud or soft and experiment making sounds at different volumes.

lessons.title: My First Instrument: Shakers and Strikers
lessons.brief: Students play simple percussion instruments like shakers and drums and discover how to make different sounds.

grade_2.focus: Music has rhythm and beat—learning to feel the pulse and move with sound.

lessons.title: What is the Beat?
lessons.brief: Students identify the steady pulse in songs and music by clapping, tapping, and moving along.

lessons.title: Fast and Slow: Tempo Changes
lessons.brief: Students experience how music can speed up or slow down and move their bodies to match the tempo.

lessons.title: Rhythm Patterns: Clap and Copy
lessons.brief: Students learn simple repeating rhythm patterns and practice copying and creating their own patterns.

lessons.title: Song and Movement
lessons.brief: Students sing familiar songs and add body movements that match the beat and rhythm.

grade_3.focus: Music uses melody and notes—learning to recognize pitch patterns and how songs are built.

lessons.title: Melody: When Notes Tell a Story
lessons.brief: Students identify the tune or melody in songs and learn that melodies are patterns of high and low notes.

lessons.title: Do Re Mi: The Scale
lessons.brief: Students learn the basic musical scale (do, re, mi, fa, sol) and sing these notes in order.

lessons.title: Reading Simple Melodies on Paper
lessons.brief: Students learn that notes on a staff show pitch (high or low) and practice reading simple melodies.

lessons.title: How Songs are Organized: Verses and Choruses
lessons.brief: Students identify and compare the repeating parts (chorus) and different parts (verses) in songs.

grade_4.focus: Music has structure and instruments—learning how musical parts fit together and what creates different sounds.

lessons.title: Instrument Families: Strings, Woodwinds, Brass, and Percussion
lessons.brief: Students explore four main instrument families, how each produces sound, and recognize them by ear.

lessons.title: Building a Song: Melody, Rhythm, and Harmony
lessons.brief: Students learn how melody (the tune), rhythm (the beat pattern), and harmony (notes played together) combine in music.

lessons.title: Dynamics and Expression: Playing with Feeling
lessons.brief: Students learn how loudness (dynamics), speed changes, and style choices shape how music sounds and feels.

lessons.title: Musical Form: How Long Songs Are Designed
lessons.brief: Students analyze song structures like verse-chorus-bridge and understand why songs are organized this way.

grade_5.focus: Music reflects culture and history—learning how music connects to people, places, and time periods.

lessons.title: Folk Music and Where It Comes From
lessons.brief: Students explore traditional music from different cultures and regions and understand what stories folk songs tell.

lessons.title: Classical Composers and Their Styles
lessons.brief: Students listen to famous composers like Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven and discover how their music changed over time.

lessons.title: Harmony in Depth: Chords and How They Sound
lessons.brief: Students learn how chords are built from multiple notes, why certain combinations sound pleasant or tense, and their use in songs.

lessons.title: Music Notation and Reading Rhythm Values
lessons.brief: Students read and write rhythms using proper notation symbols and understand how note length works.

grade_6.focus: Music connects history, culture, and emotions—analyzing how music reflects and shapes society.

lessons.title: How Music Styles Developed: Jazz, Blues, and Rock
lessons.brief: Students trace the origins and evolution of major musical genres and understand how they emerged from cultural mixing and innovation.

lessons.title: Analyzing Emotion and Meaning in Compositions
lessons.brief: Students examine how composers use tempo, dynamics, instrumentation, and harmony to express emotions and tell stories.

lessons.title: Music and Identity: Songs That Define Communities
lessons.brief: Students explore how music represents cultural identity, protest, celebration, and social change across different societies.

lessons.title: From Score to Performance: How Conductors Shape Music
lessons.brief: Students learn how conductors interpret written music and coordinate musicians to create different artistic choices and meanings.

grade_7.focus: How music reflects and shapes the societies that create it across different cultures and time periods.

lessons.title: Music as Historical Evidence
lessons.brief: Using songs, instruments, and performance styles to understand what life was like in different historical periods.

lessons.title: Cultural Identity in Sound
lessons.brief: Exploring how specific musical traditions (folk, classical, hip-hop, gamelan) connect to the values and geography of their communities.

lessons.title: The Politics of Popular Music
lessons.brief: Examining how musicians have used their platforms to challenge injustice and inspire social change from protest songs to modern activism.

lessons.title: Why Societies Value Different Instruments
lessons.brief: Investigating which instruments gain status in different cultures and what that reveals about power, religion, and wealth.

grade_8.focus: Competing claims about music's purpose: entertainment, art, social tool, or commodity—and how context determines which definition matters most.

lessons.title: Is Music an Art or a Product?
lessons.brief: Debating whether the rise of recorded music and streaming services changed music's fundamental role in society, with evidence from both sides.

lessons.title: Who Decides What Music Matters?
lessons.brief: Analyzing how gatekeepers (record labels, critics, playlists, institutions) shape which music becomes canonical and whose voices get heard.

lessons.title: Music Across the Colonial Divide
lessons.brief: Examining how colonialism exported Western musical systems while erasing indigenous traditions, and how musicians reclaim that history today.

lessons.title: The Economics of Sound: From Concert Halls to Streaming
lessons.brief: Tracing how technology and business models (concert revenue, recording, radio, streaming) have fundamentally altered how musicians survive financially.

grade_9.focus: Building a personal framework for analyzing music by synthesizing cultural, economic, technological, and aesthetic perspectives simultaneously.

lessons.title: Aesthetic vs. Commercial: Can Both Frameworks Coexist?
lessons.brief: Synthesizing ideas about artistic integrity and market forces by examining cases where musicians navigate (or reject) both demands.

lessons.title: Power and Voice: Genre as Identity and Resistance
lessons.brief: Analyzing how marginalized communities use genre creation (jazz, punk, grime, corridos) both as authentic expression and strategic claim to cultural authority.

lessons.title: Technology as Co-Creator: What Does It Change About Music?
lessons.brief: Exploring how recording, sampling, auto-tune, and AI alter not just how music is distributed but what counts as musical creation itself.

lessons.title: The Global Stage: Hybridity, Appropriation, and Respect
lessons.brief: Evaluating how global connectivity enables cross-cultural musical exchange while raising questions about credit, ownership, and cultural respect.

grade_10.focus: Interpreting primary sources and original arguments about music's nature, value, and social role across philosophy, criticism, and cultural theory.

lessons.title: Reading Music Critics: From Hanslick to TikTok
lessons.brief: Analyzing how different eras and critics have justified why certain music is 'good' or 'important,' and detecting the unstated values beneath each argument.

lessons.title: Philosophers on Music: What Makes It Matter?
lessons.brief: Engaging with texts from Plato, Schopenhauer, and modern theorists on music's unique power over emotion, meaning, and human experience.

lessons.title: The Archive Question: Whose Music Gets Preserved and Studied?
lessons.brief: Investigating institutional decisions about what music deserves scholarly attention, funding, and preservation, and the consequences of those choices.

lessons.title: Musical Notation and Power: Who Gets to Write Music Down?
lessons.brief: Analyzing how Western notation created hierarchies between oral and written traditions, and how that shaped which musics became 'legitimate.'

grade_11.focus: Critiquing competing theoretical frameworks for understanding music while building independent arguments about its meaning and function in contemporary society.

lessons.title: Deconstructing the Canon: What Does 'Classical Music' Actually Mean?
lessons.brief: Critiquing how the term 'classical' obscures history, erases non-Western traditions, and functions as a class marker—then evaluating counterarguments.

lessons.title: Authenticity as Myth: Tracing a False Concept Through Music History
lessons.brief: Dismantling the idea that 'authentic' or 'original' music exists by examining how every tradition borrows, adapts, and evolves—and why people cling to authenticity anyway.

lessons.title: Music and Neuroscience: What Can Brain Studies Actually Tell Us?
lessons.brief: Evaluating claims about music's cognitive effects by reading neuroscientific research critically and distinguishing evidence from hype and metaphor.

lessons.title: Decolonizing Musicology: Whose Frameworks Count?
lessons.brief: Examining how Western academic music theory was imposed globally and building arguments for alternative ways of analyzing, valuing, and understanding music.

grade_12.focus: Conducting independent musicological research using primary sources, theory, and evidence to construct nuanced arguments about music's cultural, economic, and epistemological significance.

lessons.title: Research Seminar: Designing Your Own Musicological Question
lessons.brief: Developing a defensible research question, identifying appropriate sources (archival, ethnographic, economic, sonic), and building a thesis argument with evidence.

lessons.title: Comparative Frameworks: Systems of Value Across Cultures and Disciplines
lessons.brief: Synthesizing musicology, ethnomusicology, philosophy, history, and economics to construct and defend a coherent framework for what makes music meaningful.

lessons.title: The Politics of Representation: Music, Media, and Knowledge Production
lessons.brief: Investigating how institutions (museums, universities, festivals, playlists) construct narratives about music and conducting a critical analysis of one case study.

lessons.title: Music and the Future: Technological, Environmental, and Social Scenarios
lessons.brief: Using historical analysis, theory, and evidence to construct reasoned arguments about how music will be created, valued, and experienced in emerging contexts.

grade_1.focus: Learning about gods and goddesses as characters with names, powers, and stories.

lessons.title: Who Are the Gods?
lessons.brief: Meet the main gods and goddesses—what they look like, what powers they have, and what they do.

lessons.title: Gods and Their Special Things
lessons.brief: Learn what each god is in charge of: Zeus and the sky, Poseidon and the sea, Aphrodite and love.

lessons.title: A God's Day: What Do They Do?
lessons.brief: Explore what the gods do, how they help or trick people, and why they matter in stories.

grade_2.focus: Following complete stories about gods and heroes, understanding what happens and why.

lessons.title: Prometheus Steals Fire
lessons.brief: A god breaks the rules to help humans; learn what he does, what happens to him, and why he did it.

lessons.title: Pandora's Box: One Choice Changes Everything
lessons.brief: Follow Pandora's story step by step and see how one action causes many consequences.

lessons.title: Heracles and His Twelve Labors
lessons.brief: A hero must complete twelve difficult tasks; discover what they are and how he overcomes each one.

lessons.title: The Tale of Persephone: Spring and Winter Explained
lessons.brief: Learn how one girl's abduction explains why seasons change and what it tells us about the gods' power.

grade_3.focus: Recognizing patterns in myths—how gods, heroes, and mortals relate to each other and to nature.

lessons.title: Gods, Heroes, and Mortals: Three Different Kinds of People
lessons.brief: Compare what makes gods immortal and powerful, heroes special and brave, and mortals ordinary and short-lived.

lessons.title: Why Do Bad Things Happen? Punishment and Revenge in Myths
lessons.brief: Explore how the Greeks explained suffering through stories of gods punishing mortals, and what those stories taught.

lessons.title: Quests and Journeys: How Heroes Prove Themselves
lessons.brief: Examine the structure of hero journeys—impossible tasks, obstacles, and what they gain by completing them.

lessons.title: Natural Wonders Explained: Myths Behind Mountains, Stars, and Monsters
lessons.brief: Investigate how the Greeks used mythology to explain real things in nature they didn't fully understand.

grade_4.focus: Understanding mythology as an interconnected system: how gods relate to each other, how myths organize the world, and how stories teach values.

lessons.title: The Family Tree of Gods: Relationships and Rivalries
lessons.brief: Map the genealogy of the Olympian gods, examine how family dynamics (alliances, conflicts, power struggles) shape divine actions.

lessons.title: The Underworld System: Death, Judgment, and the Afterlife
lessons.brief: Learn the structure of the Greek afterlife—Hades' domain, the River Styx, judgment, and different fates for different souls.

lessons.title: Hubris and Downfall: Why Pride Leads to Punishment
lessons.brief: Analyze the recurring pattern of mortals and gods overstepping boundaries, and how consequences reflect ancient Greek values.

lessons.title: Monsters as Symbols: What Giants, Gorgons, and Chimeras Represent
lessons.brief: Explore how mythological monsters embody abstract ideas—chaos, danger, the untamed—and why heroes must defeat them.

grade_5.focus: Analyzing how mythology works as a system of explanation, moral instruction, and cultural values—and how it connects to history, art, and human psychology.

lessons.title: Myth as Explanation: How Ancient Greeks Understood Cause and Effect
lessons.brief: Examine how myths answered real questions (Why do we have seasons? Why do we die? Why do we suffer?) before science existed.

lessons.title: The Hero's Journey: A Repeating Pattern Across Different Stories
lessons.brief: Identify the common sequence in hero myths—the call, the struggle, the discovery—and understand why this pattern appears in many cultures.

lessons.title: What Myths Reveal About Ancient Greek Society: Values, Rules, and Warnings
lessons.brief: Interpret what myths teach about honor, obedience, justice, and fate—and what these lessons say about Greek culture.

lessons.title: Transformations and Metamorphosis: When Gods Change Form and Identity
lessons.brief: Investigate stories of transformation (gods as animals, humans as plants) and explore what changes in identity represent symbolically.

grade_6.focus: Critically examining mythology as cultural narrative: how myths have been interpreted differently over time, how they reflect and shape worldviews, and how they remain relevant.

lessons.title: Competing Versions: Why the Same Myth Has Different Endings
lessons.brief: Compare how different ancient authors (Homer, Ovid, Hesiod) told the same story differently, and analyze what those variations reveal about perspective and change.

lessons.title: Power and Gender in Mythology: How Stories Reflected and Reinforced Social Order
lessons.brief: Critically examine how male and female gods are portrayed, what roles women and men play, and how these myths reflected Greek society's structure.

lessons.title: Myth and Truth: How the Ancient Greeks Used Stories to Make Sense of Reality
lessons.brief: Explore the relationship between mythological truth (metaphorical, moral) and literal truth (historical, factual), and why myths are powerful even if not factually true.

lessons.title: Echoes in Modern Culture: Why Ancient Myths Still Matter Today
lessons.brief: Trace how Greek mythology appears in modern literature, film, psychology (Oedipus complex), and values, and discuss why these ancient stories remain culturally significant.

grade_7.focus: Myths as windows into how ancient cultures explained the world, valued heroism, and understood human nature.

lessons.title: Why Ancient Societies Created Myths
lessons.brief: Explores how myths served as explanations for natural phenomena, social rules, and the origins of civilizations before written history and science.

lessons.title: The Hero's Journey Across Cultures
lessons.brief: Identifies the common pattern of the hero myth (call to adventure, trials, transformation, return) in Greek, Norse, Mesopotamian, and other traditions.

lessons.title: Gods and Mortals: Power and Consequence
lessons.brief: Examines how myths use divine characters to teach lessons about human ambition, pride, fate, and the boundaries between mortals and immortals.

lessons.title: Creation Myths: How Cultures Imagined the Beginning
lessons.brief: Compares creation stories from different civilizations to reveal what each culture valued most about order, chaos, family, and creation itself.

grade_8.focus: Myths as contested stories—how the same myth changes across time and cultures, and what those changes reveal about the societies that told them.

lessons.title: One Story, Many Versions: Tracing Myth Across Cultures
lessons.brief: Tracks how a single myth (e.g., the flood narrative, the underworld journey) appears in different cultures and evolves with new emphases and meanings.

lessons.title: Whose Myth Is It? Power and Narrative Control
lessons.brief: Analyzes how dominant groups shaped mythological narratives to justify power, colonialism, or social hierarchies, and how marginalized voices were silenced or rewritten.

lessons.title: Myth Versus History: Separating Legend from Fact
lessons.brief: Investigates which mythological events have archaeological or historical evidence, and why cultures blur the line between myth and history.

lessons.title: Conflict in the Myths: What Stories Reveal About Social Tensions
lessons.brief: Reads myths as reflections of real social conflicts—between genders, classes, old and new gods—embedded in narrative form.

grade_9.focus: Myths as philosophical and psychological frameworks for understanding meaning, identity, morality, and the human condition.

lessons.title: Archetypal Patterns: Jung, Campbell, and Myth as Universal Language
lessons.brief: Applies Jungian and Campbellian frameworks to identify archetypal characters and symbols (the mentor, the shadow, the threshold) that recur across mythologies.

lessons.title: Fate, Free Will, and Moral Responsibility in Mythological Narratives
lessons.brief: Examines how different mythological traditions (Greek determinism, Norse inevitability, Hindu karma) frame questions of destiny and human agency.

lessons.title: Metaphor and Meaning: Reading Myths as Symbolic Systems
lessons.brief: Decodes mythological symbols (water, descent, fire, the labyrinth) as carriers of psychological and philosophical meaning rather than literal events.

lessons.title: Myth and Identity: How Communities Construct Belonging Through Story
lessons.brief: Explores how myths function as identity narratives for cultures, nations, and groups—defining 'us' and 'them' through origin stories and heroic lineages.

grade_10.focus: Close reading of original and translated mythological texts, with attention to literary technique, cultural context, and the distance between ancient meaning and modern interpretation.

lessons.title: Reading the Iliad and Odyssey: Text, Context, and the Homeric Question
lessons.brief: Engages with excerpts from Homer's epics in translation, considers debates over authorship and oral tradition, and examines how epic conventions shape meaning.

lessons.title: Tragedy and Myth: How Greek Playwrights Rewrote Ancient Stories
lessons.brief: Analyzes how Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides adapted myths for the stage, shifting emphasis, adding psychological depth, and challenging traditional interpretations.

lessons.title: Translation, Interpretation, and Lost Nuance
lessons.brief: Compares multiple translations of the same mythological text and considers what is gained and lost in moving between languages and cultural moments.

lessons.title: Myth and Ritual: The Religious Dimensions of Ancient Narrative
lessons.brief: Connects mythological narratives to religious practices, festivals, and rituals they supported, showing how myth and worship reinforced each other.

grade_11.focus: Critical analysis of competing interpretations: how scholars, philosophers, artists, and activists have claimed, reinterpreted, and contested mythological meaning for their own purposes.

lessons.title: Myth as Ideology: From Nazi Paganism to Postcolonial Reclamation
lessons.brief: Critiques how political movements weaponized myth (Nazi appropriation of Germanic mythology, colonial erasure of indigenous myths) and how marginalized communities reclaimed mythological narratives.

lessons.title: Psychoanalytic Versus Structural Versus Feminist Readings of Myth
lessons.brief: Compares major theoretical frameworks (Freudian, Lévi-Straussian structuralism, feminist critique) applied to the same myths, evaluating their strengths and limitations.

lessons.title: Myth in Modernity: Why Artists and Writers Keep Returning to Ancient Stories
lessons.brief: Examines how 20th and 21st-century creators (Joyce, Plath, Morrison, contemporary filmmakers) rewrite myths to comment on their own time and challenge inherited meanings.

lessons.title: Demythologizing and Remythologizing: The Politics of Interpretation
lessons.brief: Argues that every reading of myth is a choice to either strip away 'false' meanings or construct new ones—and traces the power dynamics embedded in those choices.

grade_12.focus: Independent inquiry into a mythological problem or question, synthesizing historical, textual, theoretical, and creative perspectives to develop an original argument.

lessons.title: Designing a Mythological Research Question: Scope, Stakes, and Method
lessons.brief: Guides students in formulating focused research questions (e.g., 'How did Mesopotamian myths reflect economic anxiety in the Old Babylonian period?') and selecting appropriate primary and secondary sources.

lessons.title: Reading Against the Grain: Finding Silences, Contradictions, and Subtext
lessons.brief: Teaches techniques for identifying what mythological texts do *not* say, whose perspectives are absent, and how to interrogate the text's own biases and omissions.

lessons.title: Integrating Multiple Disciplines: History, Philology, Archaeology, Theory, and Creative Interpretation
lessons.brief: Shows how to build an argument that synthesizes evidence from textual analysis, historical documentation, archaeological findings, and theoretical frameworks without reducing myth to any single explanation.

lessons.title: Constructing and Defending a Thesis: Myth as Evidence and Myth as Problem
lessons.brief: Develops skills in making and supporting claims about mythological meaning while acknowledging interpretive limits, competing interpretations, and the role of the interpreter's own position.

grade_1.focus: Learning about the places and people who lived in our nation a long time ago, and what they needed to survive.

lessons.title: The First Families
lessons.brief: Meet the people who lived in our land before anyone else, and what they hunted, gathered, and built.

lessons.title: How We Know About Long Ago
lessons.brief: Discovering what old things—like stone tools, bones, and pictures—tell us about people from the past.

lessons.title: Homes Across Time
lessons.brief: Looking at the different kinds of houses people built in different places, using materials they found nearby.

grade_2.focus: Exploring different groups of people in our nation's early history and how they lived in their own ways.

lessons.title: Nations Before Nations
lessons.brief: Learning about the distinct Indigenous nations that lived across our land, each with their own languages, beliefs, and customs.

lessons.title: Living Off the Land
lessons.brief: Understanding how different groups hunted, farmed, fished, and gathered based on where they lived.

lessons.title: Telling Stories Across Time
lessons.brief: Discovering how people passed down history through spoken stories, art, and ceremonies instead of writing.

grade_3.focus: Understanding how contact between different peoples changed our nation and led to conflict, cooperation, and major shifts.

lessons.title: When Two Worlds Met
lessons.brief: Examining what happened when European explorers and settlers arrived and encountered Indigenous peoples who were already here.

lessons.title: Trade, Treaties, and Territory
lessons.brief: Comparing how some groups traded goods and signed agreements, while others fought over land and resources.

lessons.title: Forced Change and Survival
lessons.brief: Learning about the hardships Indigenous peoples faced through disease, loss of land, and pressure to change their way of life.

grade_4.focus: Analyzing how colonial systems were built, how they worked, and how they shaped the structure of our emerging nation.

lessons.title: Building Colonial Power
lessons.brief: Examining how European colonies were established, organized, and governed as part of larger empires competing for control.

lessons.title: Systems of Labor and Land
lessons.brief: Understanding the economic foundations of colonies—including slavery, indentured servitude, and the seizure of Indigenous territories.

lessons.title: Resistance and Rebellion
lessons.brief: Studying how enslaved people, servants, and Indigenous nations resisted colonial control through escapes, uprisings, and treaties.

grade_5.focus: Tracing the ideological and political movements that led to independence, revolution, and the formation of a new nation.

lessons.title: Ideas About Freedom and Rights
lessons.brief: Exploring Enlightenment philosophy and how colonists developed arguments for self-governance and individual rights, and whose rights were excluded.

lessons.title: From Tension to Revolution
lessons.brief: Following the sequence of taxes, protests, and military conflict that escalated tensions between colonies and the British Crown into armed rebellion.

lessons.title: Building the New Nation's Foundations
lessons.brief: Analyzing the choices made in early government documents and institutions, and why disagreements over slavery and representation created lasting divisions.

grade_6.focus: Investigating how political, economic, and social systems developed and competed in the early nation, and the consequences for different groups.

lessons.title: Competing Visions for the Nation
lessons.brief: Examining how different leaders and regions held conflicting ideas about federal power, slavery, westward expansion, and the role of government.

lessons.title: Expansion and Displacement
lessons.brief: Analyzing how westward movement, justified by ideology and law, systematically removed Indigenous peoples and reshaped the nation's geography and power.

lessons.title: The Economics of Slavery and Sectionalism
lessons.brief: Investigating how slavery became central to the Southern economy, deepened regional divisions, and pushed the nation toward crisis.

grade_7.focus: How did our nation form, and what were the major turning points that shaped its early identity?

lessons.title: The Foundations: From Settlement to Statehood
lessons.brief: Explores the geographic, cultural, and political conditions that led to the establishment of the nation as an independent state.

lessons.title: Conflict and Compromise: The First Century
lessons.brief: Examines the key conflicts, compromises, and decisions that defined the nation's early institutions and territorial expansion.

lessons.title: Building National Identity: Symbols, Stories, and Citizens
lessons.brief: Investigates how the nation deliberately created symbols, narratives, and citizenship concepts to unite diverse populations.

lessons.title: Whose History? Voices Left Out of the Official Story
lessons.brief: Introduces the idea that history is told from particular perspectives and asks whose stories were absent from founding narratives.

grade_8.focus: What caused the major internal conflicts in our nation's history, and what do they reveal about competing visions for what the nation should be?

lessons.title: The Ideological Divide: Freedom and Rights in Theory vs. Practice
lessons.brief: Analyzes the contradiction between the nation's founding principles and their unequal application to different groups, and how this tension sparked conflict.

lessons.title: When the Nation Split: Causes and Consequences of Internal War
lessons.brief: Examines the specific political, economic, and social grievances that led to the most serious internal conflict and what each side believed they were fighting for.

lessons.title: Reconstruction and Its Failures: Why Peace Was Harder Than War
lessons.brief: Explores how the nation attempted to reunite after internal conflict and why integration efforts fell short of their stated goals.

lessons.title: Competing Narratives: How Different Groups Remember the Same Events
lessons.brief: Compares how different communities in the nation remember and interpret pivotal conflicts based on their own historical experience.

grade_9.focus: How did the nation's economy, technology, and global role transform during the Industrial and Modern eras, and who benefited or suffered from these changes?

lessons.title: From Rural to Urban: How Industrialization Reshaped Society and Power
lessons.brief: Traces the shift from agricultural to industrial economy, examining the emergence of new classes, labor movements, and political tensions this created.

lessons.title: Empire and Influence: How the Nation Became a Global Power
lessons.brief: Analyzes the nation's military, economic, and cultural expansion internationally and the justifications offered—and critiques raised—for this expansion.

lessons.title: Rights Movements and Social Change: Who Demanded Power and How
lessons.brief: Examines organized movements for civil rights, labor rights, and social justice, comparing their strategies, opposition, and partial or complete victories.

lessons.title: Prosperity and Inequality: Whose Standard of Living Improved?
lessons.brief: Investigates economic growth and technological progress while asking which populations benefited most and least, and why.

grade_10.focus: How do we interpret conflicting primary sources and evidence to understand pivotal moments in national history, and what do our interpretations reveal about current debates?

lessons.title: Reading Against the Grain: Analyzing Official Documents and Their Silences
lessons.brief: Develops skills in close reading of primary sources—letters, laws, speeches—to identify what is claimed, what is assumed, and what is deliberately left unsaid.

lessons.title: The Same Event, Different Stories: How Historians Construct Competing Narratives
lessons.brief: Compares multiple historical interpretations of a single pivotal event, examining how source selection, emphasis, and framework shape radically different conclusions.

lessons.title: Evidence, Bias, and Certainty: What Can We Actually Know About the Past?
lessons.brief: Explores the limitations of historical evidence, the role of historian perspective, and the difference between what is known, debated, and unknowable.

lessons.title: From Then to Now: How Historical Events Are Used in Current Political Arguments
lessons.brief: Examines how politicians, activists, and citizens invoke history to support contemporary positions and analyzes when such use is accurate, misleading, or selective.

grade_11.focus: What theoretical frameworks best explain large-scale historical change, and how do different schools of historical thought challenge or support the nation's dominant narratives?

lessons.title: Competing Frameworks: Applying Marxist, Liberal, Postcolonial, and Feminist Lenses to National History
lessons.brief: Introduces major schools of historical interpretation and applies each to a central national event to demonstrate how analytical framework fundamentally shapes conclusions.

lessons.title: The Nation's Self-Mythology: How Official History Became Common Sense
lessons.brief: Critiques the process by which particular versions of national history became accepted as inevitable truth and examines how power, education, and media reinforced dominant narratives.

lessons.title: Structural Change vs. Individual Agency: What Really Drives Historical Development?
lessons.brief: Debates the degree to which history is shaped by impersonal forces (economics, geography, technology) versus conscious decisions by leaders and movements.

lessons.title: Revising the Record: When and Why Historians Change Their Minds About the Past
lessons.brief: Traces how historical interpretations of major events have shifted over decades due to new evidence, new communities telling their stories, or new theoretical approaches.

grade_12.focus: How can we construct a rigorous, evidence-based interpretation of national history that acknowledges complexity, contradiction, and the stakes of historical claims for contemporary justice and identity?

lessons.title: Research Design and Historical Argument: Building a Case From Primary Sources
lessons.brief: Develops a research project where students select sources, construct an argument about a contested historical question, and defend it against counterarguments.

lessons.title: Memory, Trauma, and Public History: Who Decides How the Nation Remembers?
lessons.brief: Examines museums, memorials, curricula, and public debates as sites where historical interpretation becomes official memory and shapes national identity and reconciliation.

lessons.title: Historiography as Philosophy: What Does It Mean to Know and Tell the Truth About the Past?
lessons.brief: Explores epistemological questions about historical knowledge—objectivity, subjectivity, truth, and the ethics of representing others' experiences and suffering.

lessons.title: The Uses and Abuses of History: When Historical Claims Enter Politics and Law
lessons.brief: Analyzes contemporary political and legal arguments grounded in historical claims, evaluating the evidence, identifying distortions, and considering the real-world consequences of historical interpretation.

grade_1.focus: Learning to notice and name the things around us, and how we use our senses and feelings to understand the world.

lessons.title: What Can We See, Hear, Touch, and Feel?
lessons.brief: Using our five senses to explore objects and the world around us, and discovering that different things feel and look different.

lessons.title: Happy, Sad, Angry, Calm: What Are Feelings?
lessons.brief: Naming basic emotions we experience and noticing what happens in our body when we feel different ways.

lessons.title: Things We Do Every Day
lessons.brief: Noticing our daily routines and how we make simple choices about what to do and when.

grade_2.focus: Exploring how things work, why we do things, and discovering that everything has a reason or a purpose.

lessons.title: Why Do We Have Rules?
lessons.brief: Learning that rules help us stay safe and get along with others, and seeing how rules work at home and at school.

lessons.title: What Makes Something Fair?
lessons.brief: Discovering what fairness means through sharing, taking turns, and treating others the way we want to be treated.

lessons.title: Real Things and Make-Believe Things
lessons.brief: Learning to tell the difference between what is real, what we can see and touch, and what we imagine or dream.

lessons.title: Does Everyone Think the Same Way?
lessons.brief: Noticing that different people like different things, have different ideas, and see things in different ways.

grade_3.focus: Sorting ideas into groups, understanding how one thing causes another, and learning that people have different beliefs and ways of living.

lessons.title: Sorting and Grouping: How Things Belong Together
lessons.brief: Classifying objects, ideas, and actions into categories and understanding why things fit into certain groups.

lessons.title: Why Did That Happen? Cause and Effect
lessons.brief: Tracing chains of causes and effects in simple events, and understanding that our choices lead to results.

lessons.title: Different Families, Different Ways of Living
lessons.brief: Exploring how families around the world live differently, eat different foods, and celebrate in different ways.

lessons.title: What Is a Belief? Comparing How People Think
lessons.brief: Introducing the idea that people believe different things about what is right, important, or true.

grade_4.focus: Understanding how parts connect to make a whole system, and recognizing that many viewpoints exist within those systems.

lessons.title: Communities as Systems: How Parts Work Together
lessons.brief: Examining how a family, school, or neighborhood is made up of parts that depend on each other and work toward shared goals.

lessons.title: Truth, Lies, and How We Know What Is Real
lessons.brief: Exploring how we decide what is true, what counts as evidence, and why people sometimes disagree about facts.

lessons.title: Rights and Responsibilities: What Do We Owe Each Other?
lessons.brief: Learning that people have rights (things they deserve), and that along with those rights come responsibilities (things they must do).

lessons.title: Cultures, Traditions, and Why They Matter
lessons.brief: Investigating how different cultures have different values, customs, and traditions that give meaning to people's lives.

grade_5.focus: Asking deeper 'why' questions about knowledge, morality, identity, and society, and recognizing that big questions often don't have simple answers.

lessons.title: What Makes Someone a Good Person?
lessons.brief: Exploring virtue, character, and moral development by examining what goodness means across different cultures and contexts.

lessons.title: How Do We Know What We Know?
lessons.brief: Investigating knowledge, reasoning, and sources of truth—how science, experience, and tradition each teach us different things.

lessons.title: Freedom, Choice, and Responsibility
lessons.brief: Examining what freedom means, how much choice we really have, and how our choices affect others in society.

lessons.title: Power, Fairness, and How Society Is Organized
lessons.brief: Analyzing why societies have leaders and rules, what makes a system fair or unfair, and who gets to decide.

grade_6.focus: Synthesizing connections across philosophical questions about existence, meaning, knowledge, and ethics, and developing personal philosophical perspectives.

lessons.title: Logic, Reasoning, and the Art of Argument
lessons.brief: Learning to construct and evaluate logical arguments, identifying fallacies, and understanding why reasoning matters in philosophy.

lessons.title: The Self: Who Am I and How Am I Different From Others?
lessons.brief: Investigating identity, consciousness, and what makes a person unique—exploring whether identity is fixed or changes over time.

lessons.title: Meaning, Purpose, and What Makes Life Worth Living
lessons.brief: Examining different perspectives on meaning—through achievement, relationships, creativity, or contribution—and what gives life value.

lessons.title: Ethics in Conflict: When Values Clash
lessons.brief: Analyzing real-world moral dilemmas where different values conflict, and developing frameworks for making difficult ethical decisions.

grade_7.focus: Learning to recognize and evaluate the big questions humans ask, and discovering that reasonable people can disagree on the answers.

lessons.title: What Makes a Question Philosophical?
lessons.brief: Distinguishing philosophical questions from factual, scientific, or opinion-based ones, and why some questions matter more than others.

lessons.title: Arguments and Evidence: Why Saying Something Doesn't Make It True
lessons.brief: Identifying the structure of arguments, spotting weak reasoning, and understanding why evidence and logic matter in debate.

lessons.title: Belief Systems Around the World
lessons.brief: Exploring how different cultures and religions answer fundamental questions about meaning, right and wrong, and how to live well.

lessons.title: The Trolley Problem and Other Moral Dilemmas
lessons.brief: Using thought experiments to discover that ethical decisions often involve competing values, and that there may be no perfect answer.

grade_8.focus: Developing the ability to construct and defend your own position on a philosophical question, while genuinely understanding the opposing view.

lessons.title: How Do We Know What's Right and Wrong?
lessons.brief: Comparing major ethical frameworks—consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics—and testing each against real-world scenarios to see which fits best.

lessons.title: Free Will vs. Determinism: Are Our Choices Really Ours?
lessons.brief: Exploring whether humans have genuine freedom or whether our actions are determined by genetics, environment, or fate, and why it matters.

lessons.title: What Can We Actually Know?
lessons.brief: Investigating the foundations of knowledge: what counts as truth, how we justify beliefs, and why certainty is harder to achieve than we think.

lessons.title: Justice: Equal Treatment or Equal Outcomes?
lessons.brief: Examining competing theories of fairness, from equal opportunity to equal resources, and testing them against concrete policy questions.

grade_9.focus: Building a coherent personal philosophical framework by synthesizing across multiple domains and recognizing how different questions connect to one another.

lessons.title: Metaphysics: What Is Real?
lessons.brief: Engaging with fundamental questions about existence, matter, mind, and whether reality is physical, mental, or both—and how this shapes ethics and knowledge.

lessons.title: The Self: Who Are You Really?
lessons.brief: Investigating personal identity, consciousness, and what makes you 'you' over time, and how different answers affect philosophy of mind and ethics.

lessons.title: Political Philosophy: Power, Rights, and the Social Contract
lessons.brief: Examining why societies exist, what justifies government authority, and how to balance individual liberty with collective welfare.

lessons.title: Meaning and Authenticity: How Should You Live?
lessons.brief: Drawing on existentialist, stoic, and virtue ethics perspectives to explore whether life has inherent meaning and how to live authentically.

grade_10.focus: Reading and interpreting primary philosophical texts, and understanding how historical thinkers built and responded to each other's arguments.

lessons.title: Plato's Cave and the Nature of Reality
lessons.brief: Close reading of Plato's allegory to understand his theory of forms, the divided line, and how he distinguishes appearance from reality.

lessons.title: Descartes' Method of Doubt and the Problem of Certainty
lessons.brief: Following Descartes' systematic skepticism to 'I think therefore I am,' and assessing whether this foundation really solves the problem of knowledge.

lessons.title: Kant's Categorical Imperative: A Universal Ethics
lessons.brief: Examining Kant's deontological approach to morality through close analysis of duty, reason, and the test of universalizability.

lessons.title: Mill and the Utilitarian Challenge to Rights
lessons.brief: Engaging with Mill's greatest happiness principle and confronting the tension between maximizing welfare and protecting individual rights.

grade_11.focus: Critically comparing major philosophical frameworks, identifying their strengths and weaknesses, and constructing original arguments that integrate multiple traditions.

lessons.title: Virtue Ethics vs. Consequentialism vs. Deontology: Which Framework Wins?
lessons.brief: Systematic comparison of three major ethical systems through their core commitments, how they resolve moral dilemmas, and their philosophical vulnerabilities.

lessons.title: The Epistemological Crisis: Can We Trust Reason, Experience, or Both?
lessons.brief: Tracing the rationalist-empiricist debate from Descartes through Hume to Kant, and evaluating contemporary responses to skepticism.

lessons.title: Critiques of Power: Marx, Foucault, and the Social Construction of Knowledge
lessons.brief: Examining how thinkers have challenged the neutrality of reason and authority, revealing how power shapes what counts as truth and justice.

lessons.title: Existentialism and Absurdism: Freedom, Responsibility, and Meaning
lessons.brief: Analyzing Sartre, Camus, and de Beauvoir on radical freedom, bad faith, and the possibility of authentic existence in a meaningless universe.

grade_12.focus: Conducting independent philosophical research, synthesizing across historical periods and cultures, and developing and defending an original thesis on a complex philosophical problem.

lessons.title: Philosophy of Mind: Consciousness, Artificial Intelligence, and the Hard Problem
lessons.brief: Integrating historical and contemporary approaches to consciousness, evaluating physicalism against dualism, and assessing whether machines can think.

lessons.title: Feminist Philosophy and Intersectional Critique of Traditional Frameworks
lessons.brief: Examining how feminist, postcolonial, and critical race theorists have revealed blind spots in canonical philosophy and reconstructed epistemology and ethics.

lessons.title: Environmental Ethics and Non-Human Moral Status
lessons.brief: Synthesizing virtue ethics, consequentialism, and indigenous philosophy to evaluate obligations to animals, ecosystems, and future generations.

lessons.title: The Limits of Language and Meaning: Wittgenstein, Poststructuralism, and Communication
lessons.brief: Exploring how language shapes thought and reality, examining deconstruction and pragmatism, and assessing what philosophy can actually claim to know or prove.

grade_1.focus: Learning to move your body in many different ways and enjoying how it feels.

lessons.title: My Body Can Move
lessons.brief: Exploring how different body parts bend, stretch, twist, and reach.

lessons.title: Walking, Running, and Jumping
lessons.brief: Practicing fast and slow ways to move across the ground.

lessons.title: Games with Friends
lessons.brief: Playing simple chasing and catching games with others.

lessons.title: Throwing and Catching a Ball
lessons.brief: Learning to throw soft balls and catch them with hands.

grade_2.focus: Controlling your body better and learning basic skills with balls and equipment.

lessons.title: Balance and Staying Still
lessons.brief: Practicing ways to stand, walk on lines, and hold positions without falling.

lessons.title: Rolling, Bouncing, and Kicking Balls
lessons.brief: Developing control when working with different sized balls.

lessons.title: Moving to Music and Rhythm
lessons.brief: Matching body movements to beats and sounds.

lessons.title: Playing Cooperatively in Small Groups
lessons.brief: Taking turns and working together in simple team activities.

grade_3.focus: Comparing different movement skills and understanding what makes some movements work better than others.

lessons.title: Agility and Change of Direction
lessons.brief: Learning how to move quickly while changing speed and direction.

lessons.title: Accuracy in Throwing and Kicking
lessons.brief: Identifying what helps a throw or kick hit a target consistently.

lessons.title: Core Strength and Stability
lessons.brief: Discovering how a strong middle body helps with balance and control.

lessons.title: Sports Rules and Fair Play
lessons.brief: Learning basic rules for games and why they keep play fair and safe.

grade_4.focus: Understanding how body systems work together to improve athletic performance and how strategy affects game outcomes.

lessons.title: How Muscles and Bones Work Together
lessons.brief: Exploring how skeletal and muscular systems enable different movements.

lessons.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Activity
lessons.brief: Comparing sustained low-intensity exercise with short bursts of intense effort.

lessons.title: Positioning and Spacing in Games
lessons.brief: Recognizing how players place themselves strategically on a playing surface.

lessons.title: Biomechanics of Throwing and Running
lessons.brief: Analyzing body angles and sequencing that make athletic movements more efficient.

grade_5.focus: Analyzing how training and conditioning build fitness over time, and applying tactical thinking to team sports.

lessons.title: Progressive Training and Overload
lessons.brief: Explaining why gradually increasing difficulty builds strength and endurance.

lessons.title: Flexibility and Range of Motion
lessons.brief: Investigating how stretching and mobility improve movement quality and reduce injury.

lessons.title: Reading the Game and Decision-Making
lessons.brief: Developing how to assess situations quickly and choose the best action in team play.

lessons.title: Energy Systems During Different Sports
lessons.brief: Distinguishing which fuel systems the body uses during sprints, distance running, and mixed activities.

grade_6.focus: Connecting physiology, psychology, and strategy to optimize performance and understand fitness as a lifestyle.

lessons.title: Periodisation and Peak Performance
lessons.brief: Examining how athletes structure training cycles to peak at the right time.

lessons.title: Nutrition, Hydration, and Recovery
lessons.brief: Analyzing how diet and rest directly influence athletic ability and injury prevention.

lessons.title: Mental Resilience and Motivation in Sport
lessons.brief: Exploring how mindset, focus, and goal-setting affect performance under pressure.

lessons.title: Biomechanical Analysis and Movement Refinement
lessons.brief: Using video and observation to identify technique flaws and design targeted corrections.

grade_7.focus: Students discover how their bodies move, develop basic fitness habits, and learn why physical activity matters for their health and mood.

lessons.title: How Your Body Systems Work During Exercise
lessons.brief: Students learn how the heart, lungs, and muscles work together when they move, and measure their own pulse and breathing rates before, during, and after activity.

lessons.title: Building Your Fitness Foundation: Strength, Speed, and Endurance
lessons.brief: Students explore four basic fitness components through practical activities and discover their own strengths and areas to develop.

lessons.title: Sport Skills Meet Real Games
lessons.brief: Students learn why technique matters in common sports and games, practice fundamental skills, and apply them in modified gameplay.

lessons.title: Why Movement Affects Your Brain and Mood
lessons.brief: Students investigate the connection between physical activity and mental health through personal reflection and peer discussion.

grade_8.focus: Students design personal fitness plans, analyze their own movement patterns, and examine how culture and identity shape what sports and activities they choose.

lessons.title: Designing a Fitness Plan That Fits Your Life
lessons.brief: Students assess their current activity level, set realistic goals, and create a 4-week plan they can actually follow outside of class.

lessons.title: How Technique Prevents Injury and Improves Performance
lessons.brief: Students analyze movement biomechanics in sports they play, identify common form mistakes, and practice corrected techniques to see the difference.

lessons.title: Sport, Culture, and Who Gets to Participate
lessons.brief: Students explore how gender, socioeconomic status, and cultural background influence access to sports and physical activities, and discuss barriers they've observed.

lessons.title: Fueling Your Body: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
lessons.brief: Students examine what athletes eat, why hydration matters, and plan realistic meals around their own activity levels and schedules.

grade_9.focus: Students synthesize fitness knowledge to evaluate training methods, analyze movement in their chosen sports more deeply, and begin to form their own approach to lifelong physical activity.

lessons.title: Which Training Methods Actually Work: Comparing Approaches
lessons.brief: Students test different conditioning methods (circuit training, interval training, steady-state), measure results, and evaluate which approach matches their goals.

lessons.title: Biomechanics and Sport Specialization: The Physics of Your Game
lessons.brief: Students analyze detailed movement patterns in a sport of their choice, use slow-motion video, and identify how physics principles apply to their own performance.

lessons.title: Mental Skills in Competition: Pressure, Focus, and Resilience
lessons.brief: Students explore visualization, self-talk, and concentration techniques through sport and non-sport contexts, and develop a personal mental strategy.

lessons.title: Building a Sustainable Activity Identity Beyond School Sport
lessons.brief: Students reflect on what physical activities genuinely interest them, investigate options available in their community, and plan how to stay active as they age.

grade_10.focus: Students read and interpret research on exercise science, construct evidence-based arguments about training and health claims, and apply nuanced understanding to their own and others' fitness choices.

lessons.title: Reading the Research: What Does the Evidence Really Say About Exercise and Health?
lessons.brief: Students examine peer-reviewed studies on physical activity and chronic disease prevention, learn to identify study limitations, and distinguish evidence from marketing claims.

lessons.title: Periodization and Long-Term Athletic Development: Planning Growth Over Years
lessons.brief: Students analyze multi-year training plans used by competitive athletes, understand why progression matters, and critique whether elite models apply to recreational athletes.

lessons.title: The Economics and Ethics of Sport: Who Profits, Who Plays, Who's Left Out
lessons.brief: Students investigate sponsorship, professional sports structures, and access inequities; they argue multiple perspectives on fairness and opportunity in athletics.

lessons.title: Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation: Evidence and Myth
lessons.brief: Students examine which injury prevention methods are supported by research, design a program for a common athletic injury, and evaluate recovery claims critically.

grade_11.focus: Students critique training frameworks, evaluate their own biases about bodies and fitness, synthesize knowledge across physiology and social science, and construct original arguments about exercise and wellbeing.

lessons.title: Comparing Training Philosophies: When and Why Different Methods Matter
lessons.brief: Students analyze competing frameworks (periodization vs. non-linear training, high-volume vs. high-intensity, sport-specific vs. general fitness) and critique the assumptions underlying each.

lessons.title: How Social Media, Marketing, and Culture Shape Body Image and Exercise Motivation
lessons.brief: Students examine how fitness narratives are constructed, analyze their own internalized beliefs about 'good' bodies and exercise, and critique harmful claims in wellness culture.

lessons.title: Physiology Across the Lifespan: Designing Activity for Aging and Adaptation
lessons.brief: Students synthesize evidence on how aging, hormones, and life stages affect performance and health, and design programs for populations beyond elite young athletes.

lessons.title: Independent Sport Research Project: Designing and Conducting a Small Study
lessons.brief: Students formulate a research question about exercise or performance, design a method, collect data, analyze results, and present original findings with critical reflection.

grade_12.focus: Students conduct independent research, synthesize across physiology, psychology, sociology, and biomechanics, and develop evidence-based positions on complex issues in sport, health, and human performance.

lessons.title: Advanced Research Seminar: Investigating Frontiers in Exercise Science
lessons.brief: Students select, review, and critically analyze 5–8 recent peer-reviewed articles on a topic of choice, identify methodological strengths and weaknesses, and synthesize findings into a research proposal.

lessons.title: The Doping Question: Science, Ethics, and Policy in Sport
lessons.brief: Students examine pharmacology of performance-enhancing drugs, analyze arguments from athletes/scientists/policy makers on different sides, and construct an informed position on regulation and fairness.

lessons.title: Disability, Adaptation, and Sport: Reimagining What Performance Means
lessons.brief: Students synthesize biomechanics, physiology, and social justice frameworks; they examine para-sport technology and policy, challenge assumptions about 'normal' bodies, and argue about inclusion.

lessons.title: Capstone: Personal Movement Philosophy and Practice
lessons.brief: Students synthesize 6 years of learning to articulate their own framework for physical activity, health, and wellbeing; they design a realistic long-term practice and defend their approach with evidence and reflection.

grade_1.focus: Discovering how things move and change in the world around us using our senses.

lessons.title: Things That Move
lessons.brief: Observing and naming different ways objects move: rolling, sliding, bouncing, spinning.

lessons.title: Push and Pull
lessons.brief: Feeling and experimenting with forces—how pushing and pulling makes things start, stop, or change direction.

lessons.title: Hot and Cold
lessons.brief: Experiencing temperature through touch and noticing how heat makes things change: ice melts, water boils, food cooks.

lessons.title: Light and Shadow
lessons.brief: Playing with light sources and shadows to see how light travels and what blocks it.

grade_2.focus: Describing how forces affect movement and how energy appears in everyday situations.

lessons.title: Fast and Slow
lessons.brief: Comparing speeds of different objects and understanding that movement can be faster or slower.

lessons.title: Gravity Pulls Everything Down
lessons.brief: Observing how objects fall and discovering that an invisible force pulls things toward Earth.

lessons.title: Magnets Attract and Repel
lessons.brief: Experimenting with magnets to see what they pull toward them and what pushes away.

lessons.title: Sound Comes from Vibrations
lessons.brief: Making and hearing sounds, then feeling vibrations to understand where sounds come from.

grade_3.focus: Categorizing forces and energy, and explaining how they cause changes we observe.

lessons.title: Friction Slows Things Down
lessons.brief: Comparing how objects move on different surfaces and discovering that friction is a force that stops motion.

lessons.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
lessons.brief: Identifying levers, ramps, and pulleys in everyday life and seeing how they reduce the effort needed to lift or move things.

lessons.title: Energy Changes Form
lessons.brief: Observing how energy moves from one place to another: light becomes heat, moving things have energy, food gives us energy.

lessons.title: The Cycle of Day and Night
lessons.brief: Connecting Earth's rotation to the pattern of light and darkness and temperature changes throughout the day.

grade_4.focus: Understanding how forces, motion, and energy work together in systems and machines.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion in Action
lessons.brief: Experimenting with inertia, acceleration, and action-reaction pairs to explain how objects behave when forces act on them.

lessons.title: Energy Transfer Through Systems
lessons.brief: Tracing how energy flows through everyday systems: cars, bicycles, roller coasters, and water wheels.

lessons.title: Waves: Sound and Light
lessons.brief: Investigating how sound and light travel in waves and understanding frequency and amplitude.

lessons.title: Earth's Magnetic Field and Gravity
lessons.brief: Exploring how magnetism and gravity act as invisible forces across distances and keep systems in balance.

grade_5.focus: Analyzing how energy is conserved, transformed, and used in natural and human-made systems.

lessons.title: Thermal Energy and Heat Transfer
lessons.brief: Investigating conduction, convection, and radiation to explain how heat moves and changes temperature.

lessons.title: Mechanical Advantage and Efficiency
lessons.brief: Calculating how simple and complex machines reduce force requirements while exploring why real machines never reach 100% efficiency.

lessons.title: Electricity and Circuits
lessons.brief: Building series and parallel circuits to understand current flow, resistance, and how electrical energy powers devices.

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources
lessons.brief: Comparing how different energy sources (fossil fuels, solar, wind, hydro) work and their impact on energy systems.

grade_6.focus: Synthesizing how energy, forces, and matter interact at different scales and in interconnected systems.

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy Across Systems
lessons.brief: Applying the law of conservation of energy to explain transformations in mechanical, thermal, electrical, and chemical systems.

lessons.title: Waves, Frequency, and Information
lessons.brief: Analyzing how different types of waves (light, sound, electromagnetic) carry information and understanding the electromagnetic spectrum.

lessons.title: Forces at a Distance: Gravity and Electromagnetism
lessons.brief: Exploring how gravitational and electromagnetic forces operate without direct contact and shape large-scale structures.

lessons.title: Sustainability and Energy Efficiency
lessons.brief: Evaluating real-world energy systems and designing solutions for reducing waste and increasing efficiency in homes and communities.

grade_7.focus: Physics describes how things move and interact through forces, energy, and simple machines.

lessons.title: Forces Change Motion
lessons.brief: Students explore how pushes and pulls (forces) change the speed and direction of moving objects, using Newton's First and Second Laws.

lessons.title: Energy Transfers in Action
lessons.brief: Students investigate how energy moves between objects and transforms (kinetic to potential, heat, light) in everyday systems.

lessons.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
lessons.brief: Students build and test levers, pulleys, ramps, and other simple machines to discover how they reduce the effort needed to do work.

grade_8.focus: Physics explains motion and forces using mathematical relationships and laws that hold everywhere.

lessons.title: Measuring Motion Precisely
lessons.brief: Students quantify speed, velocity, and acceleration, then use graphs and equations to predict where objects will be.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws Govern All Motion
lessons.brief: Students apply the three laws of motion to real systems (collisions, friction, orbits) and debate why Newton's framework has held for 300 years.

lessons.title: Momentum and Collisions
lessons.brief: Students discover that momentum is conserved in collisions and use this principle to analyze car crashes, explosions, and athletic impacts.

lessons.title: Waves Carry Energy
lessons.brief: Students measure wavelength, frequency, and amplitude, then explore how sound and water waves transport energy without moving matter.

grade_9.focus: Physics connects motion, forces, and energy through mathematical laws, revealing the unity beneath diverse phenomena.

lessons.title: Work, Power, and Efficiency
lessons.brief: Students calculate work and power in real machines, then evaluate why no machine is 100% efficient and where lost energy goes.

lessons.title: Gravity: From Apples to Orbits
lessons.brief: Students derive and apply Newton's law of universal gravitation, explaining both why objects fall on Earth and why planets stay in orbit.

lessons.title: Resonance and Standing Waves
lessons.brief: Students investigate how waves reinforce themselves at certain frequencies, leading to resonance, and examine why buildings collapse or bridge designs fail.

lessons.title: Electricity as Flow and Force
lessons.brief: Students model electric current as moving charges, calculate resistance and power in circuits, and predict circuit behavior using Ohm's and Joule's laws.

grade_10.focus: Physics unifies electricity, magnetism, and light as manifestations of a single electromagnetic phenomenon, governed by fields.

lessons.title: Electric Fields and Potentials
lessons.brief: Students transition from force-based thinking to field-based thinking, using field lines and potential energy to visualize and predict electric behavior.

lessons.title: Magnetism Emerges from Moving Charges
lessons.brief: Students discover that magnetic fields arise from electric currents, calculate magnetic forces on moving charges, and analyze how motors and generators exploit this relationship.

lessons.title: Induction: The Bridge Between Electricity and Magnetism
lessons.brief: Students apply Faraday's law to explain how changing magnetic fields generate electric currents, then design transformers and analyze energy transmission.

lessons.title: Light as Electromagnetic Waves
lessons.brief: Students interpret Maxwell's equations (conceptually), recognize light as an electromagnetic wave, and explain reflection, refraction, and interference using wave properties.

grade_11.focus: Physics reveals that space, time, and energy are interwoven; matter and radiation obey quantum and relativistic principles at extreme scales.

lessons.title: Special Relativity Challenges Space and Time
lessons.brief: Students derive and critique Einstein's postulates, explore time dilation and length contraction, and synthesize E=mc² with conservation laws to understand relativistic momentum and energy.

lessons.title: Photons and the Quantum Leap
lessons.brief: Students analyze the photoelectric effect and atomic spectra as evidence for quantized energy, then compare classical and quantum interpretations to evaluate why both frameworks have merit.

lessons.title: The Nucleus: Binding Energy and Radioactivity
